entry.title: Learning SAP Build Process Automation: My Beginner Guide & Hands-on Practice (Part 2/2)
entry.content:
Let’s begin the Part 2! In [Part 1 (link to Part 1)], we set up our Control Tower environment, built our employee trigger form, mapped process variables, and created a simple manager approval step.

Now, we are going to make our workflow smarter and more dynamic.

In this post, we will cover two main enhancements:

  • Task 2: Adding explicit Approval and Rejection confirmation forms.
  • Task 3: Implementing Conditional Branch Logic (Controls) to route requests automatically!

Trigger Form Reference

Just as a quick reminder from Part 1, here are the fields we configured in our initial Trigger Form:

The Business Rules We Are Building

Before jumping into the canvas, let's look at the exact approval conditions we want our system to enforce.

 

Task 2: Enhanced Process (Adding Approval & Rejection Forms)

Instead of the process simply ending after a manager clicks approve or reject, we want to provide clear confirmation forms back to the employee.

Step 1: Create Confirmation Forms

  1. In your process canvas, add two new forms:
    • PR Approved Form
    • PR Rejected Form
  2. In each form editor, add headers and text fields displaying the Trigger Form details (e.g., Employee Name, Amount, Purchase Date) and set them to Read-Only.
  3. Add a clear callout message at the top (e.g., "Your purchase requisition has been approved!" or "Your purchase requisition has been rejected.").

Step 2: Connect Forms to Manager Approval Outcomes

  1. In the process builder, connect the Approve branch of the Manager Approval step to your PR Approved Form.
  2. Connect the Reject branch to your PR Rejected Form.
  3. Ensure all process inputs are mapped correctly to both forms in the Inputs tab.

Step 3: Release, Deploy & Test Version 2

  1. Click Release → Choose Version 2 → Deploy to your Control Tower environment.
  2. Open the Trigger Form link in a new tab and submit a test request.
  3. Open My Inbox, approve the request, and verify that the approval confirmation form triggers as expected!

 

Task 3: Adding Conditional Logic for Auto-Approvals

Now let's add automated decisions so managers don't waste time manually reviewing small, low-value purchase requests.

Step 1: Add a Controls Step (Branching Logic)

  1. In your process flow, click (+) right after the Trigger step and select Controls → Condition.
  2. Configure the branches as follows:
    1. If Branch: Priority = Urgent AND Amount (USD) = 100 OR Amount (USD) = 100
    2. Default Branch: (Leave as Default for all other inputs) 

Step 2: Configure the Auto-Approval Form

  1. Drag the Auto-Approval Form onto the If branch.
  2. Map all request details (Employee Name, Amount, Purchase Date, Priority) from the trigger step to the form fields as Read-Only.
  3. Set the Subject line to: AUTO-APPROVED: Purchase Request for [Employee Name].
  4. Set Recipients to Started By (for testing purposes).
  5. Connect the Default branch directly to your existing Manager Approval step.

Step 3: Release, Deploy, and Execute Final End-to-End Testing!

Release Version 3 of your process, deploy it to your environment, and test these three scenarios to ensure your logic works seamlessly:

Scenario

Inputs to Fill

Where to Verify

Amount = $50

Bypasses manager review → Triggers Auto-Approval Form

My Inbox

Test B: Manager Review

Amount = $500

Sent to Manager Approval task

My Inbox (Click Approve/Reject)

Test C: Auto-Rejection

Amount = $1,600

Bypasses manager review → Triggers PR Rejected Form

My Inbox

 

Key Takeaways & Conclusion

By walking through this hands-on tutorial, we have built a fully functional, dynamic business process from scratch:

  • Stage 1: Basic form-to-manager workflow.
  • Stage 2: Complete end-to-end user notifications.
  • Stage 3: Automated, rule-based branching logic.

All of this was accomplished without writing a single line of code!

I hope this beginner guide helps you feel much more confident when taking on SAP Build Process Automation exercises. 

 

Reference

SAP. (n.d.). Developing with SAP Build – From Apps to Automation [Learning journey]. SAP Learning. Retrieved July 25, 2026, from https://learning.sap.com/learning-journeys/developing-with-sap-build-from-apps-to-automation

entry.title: August Developer Challenge Week 4 - Vercel
entry.content:
The challenge is now closed. You can still perform the challenge, but no additional badges will be awarded. A summary of how we awarded badges and who completed ALL the tasks are shown in our blog post August Developer Challenge - NOW CLOSED.

This is part of the August Developer Challenge on Joule Studio.

SAP and Vercel have partnered to enable developers to build lightning-fast, modern frontends (using React and Next.js) for enterprise applications and AI agents, while securely connecting to SAP’s robust backend infrastructure in the newly announced Joule Studio. Vercel will become available within Joule Studio to give developers an unparalleled choice for custom frontend design. Hence, now let’s understand what Vercel, Next.js and v0 are, how they are connected to each other, and how they relate to the new Joule Studio. 

 I. Next.js: 

Next.js is a React framework for building full-stack web applications. Created by Vercel, this framework takes the power of React.js which is a popular library for building dynamic user interfaces, and supercharges it with features like server-side rendering (SSR), static site generation (SSG), and a built-in routing system, all out of the box. Developers can rapidly build highly flexible, custom web interfaces using popular frameworks like Next.js using the new Joule Studio platform. 

Let's create a new Next.js app from scratch to see it in action: 

1. System requirements: 

  • Minimum Node.js version: 20.9, install from here: https://nodejs.org/en/download . Check with node –v  command on your terminal to see the current node version installed.
  • Operating systems: macOS, Windows or Linux 
  • Git installed 
  • VS Code or another code editor with integrated terminal or a standalone terminal such as PowerShell on Windows or Terminal App/iTerm on Mac OS 
  • A GitHub Account 

2. Run these commands one by one on the terminal: 

npx create-next-app@latest business-card-app --yes 
cd business-card-app 
npm run dev

npx is a powerful tool bundled with Node.js that executes JavaScript packages directly from the registry without requiring you to install them globally 

create-next-app is the official command-line interface (CLI) tool used to instantly bootstrap and set up a new Next.js application 

npm is a command-line tool used by developers to install, share, and manage project dependencies. It is automatically installed whenever you download Node.js. 

--yes skips prompts using saved preferences or defaults. The default setup enables TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, ESLint, App Router, and Turbopack. 

  • View the business-card-app at the http://localhost:3000 url 
  • Optionally, you may use this link to the Quick Start guide from Next.js https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started to increase your understanding of the framework and explore the various possibilities. 

3. Open the project folder in VS Code and observe the folder structure (app, public folders): Next.js uses file-system based routing, meaning you can use folders and files to define routes. 

  • View the code in the layout.tsx file contents in the app folder 
  • View the code in the page.tsx file contents in the app folder 
  • View the package.json file contents at the root level 

 A .tsx file is a TypeScript source file that contains JSX, an XML-like  syntax used to describe UI in React.  

 4. Replace the contents of the page.tsx with the below content 

  • Copy code from gist here and overwrite the code in page.tsx 
  • https://gist.github.com/neelamegams/c43329a01aa0a8ee288adeb4bb4bdf2e  

5. In the newly updated page.tsx code, scroll to the bottom of the file. 

  • Search for type="hidden" within the form tag in the page.tsx. Replace the hidden values for communityId with your SAP Community username by updating the value attribute. 
  • Replace the value attributes: 
    • communityId: your SAP Community username 
    • answer: your answer to the below question (one word answer)
    • week: keep as "week4" 

S-User, P-User, the email associated with SAP Community portal are not valid Community Ids. To get your SAP Community Id, follow the instructions as per the screenshot below. 

Question: When frameworks use server-side rendering, the server delivers raw, non-interactive HTML to the browser. Name the process that attaches event listeners to this static HTML inside the browser to make the page interactive. 

  • View the business-card-app at the http://localhost:3000 url 
  • Stop the local development server by pressing Ctrl+C (Mac/Windows/Linux) in the terminal before continuing to the next steps. 

 6. Commit and push these changes to your GitHub repository. In the next step, we shall deploy this app to Vercel.  

  • If you are new to git, here is a link with video instructions on how to use git to push your code to a remote GitHub repo with VS Code editor. https://code.visualstudio.com/docs/sourcecontrol/overview 

II. Vercel 

Vercel is a cloud platform for developers that provides the infrastructure to host, build, and deploy web applications instantly. You can easily link your GitHub repository to Vercel and deploy those GitHub projects. Once deployed, you can view your site/app from a live URL hosted on the Vercel platform. 

1. Sign up to the Vercel platform from https://vercel.com/signup 

2. Choose the Continue with GitHub option and use the same GitHub account that you pushed your repository to in the previous step. Once logged in, add a new project using the Add New option in the top right corner. 

Here is a short video showing how to link your GitHub repository to Vercel https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GthkPo8xFqQ 

3. Your newly created GitHub repository is available for import to Vercel. Click on Import. 

4. Expand the Environment variables and provide the CAP_SERVICE_URL as 

https://community-challenge.cfapps.us10.hana.ondemand.com and Click Deploy. 

5. It only takes a few minutes to deploy your app. You could notice how easily you were able to deploy an app to Vercel. As soon as it is deployed, your site is live. You will be able to view your business card app with a URL unique to your deployment. 

6a: Test Your Deployment (Required) 

  1. Launch your Vercel URL in a browser 
  2. Click the SAP Community button to submit your Week 4 answer 
  3. You should see a success message confirming submission 
  4. Post a comment on this blog post with: 
    • A screenshot showing your deployed business-card-app URL in browser 

6b: Enhance Your Card (Optional ) 

Want to customize further? Edit lines in page.tsx containing: 

  • Your name and title 
  • GitHub profile URL (replace https://github.com) 
  • LinkedIn profile URL (replace https://linkedin.com) 

Commit and push to GitHub. Vercel auto-deploys changes in less than 2 minutes. Refresh your Vercel URL to see updates. 

7. Add a comment answering at least 2 of these: 

  • Ease of use: How smooth was Next.js setup and Vercel deployment? 
  • Pain points: Where did you get stuck or confused? 
  • Comparison: Do you use React/Vue/Angular or Netlify/AWS Amplify or some other tool that does something similar? How does this compare? 
  • Future use: Would you use Next.js + Vercel for your projects? Why/why not? 

III. v0 in Vercel 

v0 empowers anyone to build functional web applications faster without writing code manually. v0 generates production-ready UI components and frontend code, utilizing a modern web stack that includes Next.js, React architecture, Tailwind CSS, shadcn/ui, and the Vercel AI SDK. The code generated is ready to be deployed on the Vercel's globally scalable infrastructure. 

What is Vercel's relationship with v0?  

Vercel created v0 and provides the underlying infrastructure. This deep integration enables one-click deployment to enterprise-grade infrastructure, adhering to compliance, strong security, and global scalability. v0's code is optimized for the Vercel platform, ensuring a smooth path from idea to production.  

In the first Next.js exercise, you manually created the app and updated the page.tsx with the code provided in the exercise. You would further enhance the pages by editing the code manually without v0.  

With v0, you will be able to provide prompts to create such UIs or modify existing code imported from an existing GitHub repository.  

Joule Studio embeds Vercel's vibe-coding platform v0 natively in the browser, so users can generate modern, powerful React/Next.js front-end applications without ever leaving the Studio. 

This exercise below about v0 is an optional exercise. We included it here because v0 is the key part of Vercel that will be embedded into Joule Studio. 

Note: Though vibe-coding is a key feature in v0, we are not asking you to do vibe-coding in this exercise because you get $5 credit per month in the free trial account and you would likely expend that very quickly. 

Optional Exercise: 

  1. Open the url https://v0.app/ in a browser 
  2. You will see a text area where you can provide your prompt to vibe-code your app idea.  
  3. Just below the text area, you will see the already available templates of the sites built by vibe-coding with v0 
  4. Open the template with the title Optimus - The AI platform to build and ship and scroll through the page and access various tabs within this site 
  5. Custom landing pages such as these can be created with vibe-coding on the v0 app. You can also use v0 to build anything, from landing pages, dashboards, e-commerce stores, and AI apps to full-stack applications.

In short: 

Vercel provides the deployment and hosting platform, while v0 is the AI-powered vibe-coding tool used to generate React and Next.js applications from natural language prompts.

entry.title: SAP EMEA Business AI Agent Hackathon 2026 - Our Runners-up Medal Winning SAP Joule Agent
entry.content:
Background and Context – Why we need an agent or Why we choose this use case for the AI Hackathon

As we transition legacy Microsoft AX entities into SAP-managed S/4HANA Private cloud operations, invoice traceability has become increasingly complex. A single AX invoice can be distributed across multiple SAP Credit memo requests (CMRs) while multiple AX invoices may be consolidated and subsequently split while handling customer returns in Order to Cash function.

Key Unanswered questions to business to ensure TLS needs

  • Which SAP invoice corresponds to a specific AX invoice.
  • Which credit memo in SAP relates to the original AX invoice transaction.
  • Whether all financial documents have been correctly reconciled before month-end close.

As a result, business users frequently face challenges:

  • No system-controlled SAP–AX invoice linkage → manual reconciliation and poor scalability (For 7-10 markets approx. 30K lines )
  • Hard to connect invoice lineage → higher reconciliation effort and reduced accuracy. (2 person for 5 days)
  • Reference-based invoice matching → no automated traceability across systems.

What Agentic Capabilities – Invoice Reconciliation Agent to help Order To Cash

Objective 1 – Invoice Reference Identification and Assignment. Automatically identify and recommend invoice-to-credit memo matches, reducing manual reconciliation effort and spreadsheet analysis.
Key Outcomes

  1. AI-recommended invoice references for Credit Memo Requests (CMRs)
  2. Confidence score and match rationale for each recommendation
  3. Human approval workflow for low-confidence or exception scenarios
  4. Reduced manual effort and faster credit memo processing

 

Objective 2 – Compliance and Traceability of Credit Memo Processing Ensure every credit memo is linked to the correct original invoice, providing end-to-end traceability, statutory compliance, and audit-ready documentation.
Key Outcomes

  1. Enable accurate invoice references for statutory compliance.
  2. Improve consistency and transparency across countries and systems.
  3. Reduce compliance risk and support audit readiness.

Agentic Outcomes – Demo how the "Agent and User Interaction

As a Customer Relationship Associate, we wanted the AI agent to automatically identify and explain invoice relationships across SAP and AX so that reconciliation becomes faster, more accurate, and fully traceable.

The How – Creative Approach followed to build Joule Agent

The setup is mostly self-explanatory, detailing what was built and how.  Two things to mark specifically is the AI Core Document Pipeline and CAPM staging application. 

AI Core Document pipeline was built so that the SAP Joule Agent can reference and ingest the AX data (Exported as Excel file) to reconcile the data with SAP Data. 

Also, we did not want to give the ability to the Agent to post any data in SAP directly and keeping the "Human in Loop" SAP AI principle in mind we build the CAPM Application. 

The agent on successful execution would stage the data in the CAPM application (there is SAP HANA cloud behind it) and the user will have to make the final decision to Approve, reject or even could correct the data manually in the CAPM application before final posting in SAP. 

Taking the Joule Agent to Production

 As the agent was built over 2-3 days during the Hackathon session.  The agent needs to be enhanced with additional functionality and functional specs to match the exact business requirements.  The agent in its Hackathon stage, of course doesn't meet the business requirement as we simplified the agent build and the reasoning and the functional spec logic.  Also, the final design may be a better version of this.  I understand there may be other ways of tackling this business problem, but this was our approach to validate how SAP Business AI and SAP Joule Studio can be leveraged to help users to minimize manual efforts at the month end. 

Also, the MCP server which was built and hosted on the SAP Cloud foundry runtime, may be deployed on the MCP gateway on SAP CPI as it has now been released in the final version. 

Taking a SAP Joule agent to production is a phased, controlled journey rather than a single cutover, one that de-risks the rollout at every stage:

  1. Validate & Enhance - Validate the agent and add features to meet user-acceptance needs (UAT), ensuring it genuinely performs before moving further.
  2. Enable Governance - complete the change impact assessment and onboard end users, so the organization is prepared operationally, not just technically.
  3. Controlled Rollout - Deploy in a controlled manner to the next target market, rather than a broad, uncontrolled release.

This validate-govern-rollout approach ensures the agent earns production trust incrementally, reducing risk while building confidence at every stage of adoption.

 

Note: All text has been handwritten, Generative AI has not been used to create the diagrams or write the article.

entry.title: Bridging the Gap: SAP AI Core vs. Model Context Protocol (MCP) in SAP Build
entry.content:
As enterprise AI matures, developers and architects are constantly looking for the most efficient, secure, and scalable ways to connect Large Language Models (LLMs) to their business data.

If you are building low-code/no-code applications using SAP Build, you have likely run into two different schools of thought:

  1. The Native SAP Route: Leveraging SAP AI Core and SAP AI Launchpad (via the Generative AI Hub).
  2. The Open-Standard Route: Utilizing Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to orchestrate AI tools and data access.

At first glance, these two approaches might seem to compete. You might ask: "If I already have a robust MCP server acting as a secure gatekeeper for my data, why do I need SAP AI Core at all?"

Let’s dive into the architectural realities of both, how they handle governance, and how to choose the right path for your SAP Build projects.

The Contenders: What Do They Actually Do?

1. SAP AI Core & Launchpad: The Enterprise AI Backbone

SAP AI Core is SAP’s native infrastructure engine for running, scaling, and managing AI models within the SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP). Together with SAP AI Launchpad (the administrative control center), it provides the Generative AI Hub—a secure gateway to top-tier foundation models (like GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini) pre-configured with enterprise-grade data privacy.

2. MCP (Model Context Protocol): The Open-Standard Gatekeeper

Developed as an open standard, MCP allows developers to build secure, modular servers that expose specific data sources and tools to LLMs. Instead of giving an LLM free rein over your backend, an MCP server acts as a strict API proxy. The LLM can only interact with the exact schemas, tools, and databases that your MCP server explicitly exposes.

The Governance Showdown: Two Paths to the Same Goal

Both architectures place a massive emphasis on governance and security, but they approach it from different angles:

Feature MCP Servers (Open-Standard) SAP AI Core (Native BTP)
Control PointDeveloper-Defined: You write the code to explicitly expose only the tools and data schemas the LLM is allowed to touch.Platform-Defined: Built-in enterprise data masking, tenant isolation, and strict compliance policies (GDPR, SOC2).
MaintenanceSelf-Managed: Your team is responsible for hosting, scaling, securing, and auditing the MCP server infrastructure.SAP-Managed: SAP handles the infrastructure, security patching, scaling, and compliance certifications out of the box.
IntegrationCustom APIs: Requires exposing the MCP server securely to the internet and configuring custom API destinations in SAP Build.Native Destinations: Seamlessly integrates with SAP Build Apps and Process Automation via native BTP destinations and SSO.

Why You Might Not Need SAP AI Core (The Case for MCP)

If you are a hands-on developer or part of an agile team with strong infrastructure capabilities, MCP servers are incredibly powerful.

  • Absolute Granular Control: You act as the ultimate gatekeeper. The LLM cannot access a single byte of backend data unless your MCP server explicitly permits it.
  • Flexibility: You aren't locked into any specific cloud ecosystem. You can run your MCP servers locally, on AWS, Azure, or on-premise.
  • Rapid Prototyping: For custom developer workflows, local testing, and highly specialized tool-calling, MCP offers an elegant, lightweight developer experience.

Why Enterprise IT Prefers SAP AI Core (The Case for Native)

While MCP is brilliant for custom control, large-scale enterprises often face hurdles when managing dozens of self-hosted MCP servers. This is where SAP AI Core shines:

  1. Zero-Trust Data Privacy: The Generative AI Hub guarantees that your business data is never used to train public LLMs. It automatically handles data masking and encryption without you having to write a single line of security code.
  2. Unified Monitoring (AI Launchpad): If five different departments are building SAP Build apps, how do you track token usage, costs, and latency? SAP AI Launchpad gives IT administrators a single dashboard to monitor and budget all AI consumption across the entire enterprise.
  3. No Infrastructure Overhead: You don't have to worry about hosting, scaling GPUs, or maintaining uptime for your custom servers. SAP manages the entire lifecycle.

The Verdict: Which Should You Choose?

The choice between MCP and SAP AI Core isn't necessarily an "either/or" decision—it depends on your organizational strategy:

  • Choose MCP if you want maximum architectural flexibility, have the resources to host and secure your own middleware, and want absolute, code-level control over how your LLMs interact with your custom tools.
  • Choose SAP AI Core if you are building production-grade applications in SAP Build that require instant compliance, native BTP security, zero-maintenance infrastructure, and centralized cost monitoring.

The Hybrid Future: In many modern architectures, these technologies can even work together. You can use SAP AI Core to securely access foundation models via the Generative AI Hub, while using your custom MCP servers to safely expose specific, non-SAP legacy databases to those models.

What is your take? Are you leaning toward open-standard MCP servers for your AI integrations, or does the out-of-the-box compliance of SAP AI Core make it the winner for your SAP Build projects? Let’s discuss in the comments below!

entry.title: AI-Powered Forecasting with SAC, SAP RPT & Gen AI - Part 5: Ask, Click, or Wait
entry.content:
Part 4 got the pipeline live behind one API. This post covers three different front doors onto that same backend: a conversational Joule Skill, an embedded SAC widget with real write-back, and a scheduled notification that runs without anyone asking at all.

One backend, several front doors
Nothing about the underlying intelligence changes depending on how it's reached. The whole stack from Parts 2 to 4 stays fixed: What differs across the three options below is purely how it's reached, not the engine behind it.

Option 1: Conversational, a Joule Skill
The experience: the pipeline exposed as a custom Joule Skill, a natural-language question, "What's the recommended spend spread for project X?", typed into Joule, answered with the AI-generated narrative in plain conversation. SAP's own documentation lists the surfaces as "SAP Build Work Zone, SAP S/4HANA, SAP SuccessFactors, and other Joule-enabled applications" (however, SAC isn't named there explicitly). No navigation, no dashboard, no separate tool to open.

The scenario this was actually built for: a planner mid-way through a SAC Planning input story, wanting a quick sanity check before committing numbers, asking Joule the same question above, getting the narrative back inline, and going straight back to planning. Not a report run separately, but a question answered mid-task. Whether that's actually achievable today is genuinely unclear: see the honest gap at the end of this section before assuming it works.

  1. Create a BTP Destination connecting Joule Studio to the deployed backend, secured with a static API key kept out of visible configuration.
    • In the BTP Cockpit, under Connectivity, select Destinations and click Create.
    • Fill in Name, Description, Proxy Type as Internet, Type as HTTP, and the backend's URL: https://capstone-respread-api.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com.
    • Set Authentication to No Authentication, a POC choice, but also a requirement: a custom header added any other way gets silently dropped otherwise. 
    • Under Additional Properties, add the key exactly as URL.headers.X-Api-Key: that specific naming is what BTP Destinations require for a custom header, or it's silently ignored.
    • Click Create, then Check Connection.
    • Expose it to SAP Build, a separate step from creating it: add sap.applicationdevelopment.actions.enabled: true and sap.processautomation.enabled: true under Additional Properties, then in the SAP Build Lobby go to Control Tower → Destinations, Add, select the Destination, Next, and pick the Shared Environment the Skill will deploy to. (If that Environment doesn't exist yet: Control Tower → Environments → Add Environment, create a Shared environment; it has to exist before this step, not just before the final Skill deployment.)
  2. Import an Action from the backend's own auto-generated OpenAPI spec: this is what tells Joule what the backend can actually do.
    • It's an upload flow, not a URL-import flow: visit https://<your-app>/openapi.json in a browser first and save that file locally, then run it through the conversion script further down this post (the OpenAPI 3.1 → 3.0 fix): the next step needs the converted file, not just a link to the live spec.
    • In SAP Build, under the Connectors section, select Action and create a new connection of type API Specification, then upload the converted JSON file.
    • Check the Input and Output sections match what the backend actually expects and returns, then test the connection by passing a real API key and a real project ID as parameters, confirming the Action reaches the live endpoint before wiring anything downstream to it.
    • Release and publish the Action once the test succeeds: it isn't usable by a Skill until it's published.
  3. Wrap the Action in a Skill:
    • Create a new project of type Agent and Skill.
    • Create a new Skill with an appropriate name and description.
    • Under the skill’s settings, disable “Allow Joule to generate a response” and enable “Allow skill to be started directly by the user,” mapped so Joule’s own LLM displays the backend’s narrative verbatim rather than rewriting or re-summarizing it. Not a minor setting: rewriting it would undo every constraint built into the narrative prompt in Part 3, including the “quote the actual interval, don’t paraphrase it” rule.
    • Under Parameters, create a new skill input with an appropriate description: this is what lets Joule map a user’s natural-language project reference to the actual parameter the Action needs.
    • Add a Call Action node right after the skill trigger.
    • In the Call Action's properties, select the Destination Variable as the Destination exposed to SAP Build in step 1.
    • Map the skill input to the Action’s project_id input.
    • On the End step, explicitly map the Action’s outputs back to the skill’s outputs, a separate, easy-to-miss step from adding the Call Action node itself; skipping it means the skill runs the API call but never actually surfaces the result.
    • On a successful API call, show the narrative response as a message to the user. On failure, show an appropriate error message. 
    • Release, then Deploy: choose the target environment and click Upgrade, and match the destination binding to the Shared Environment’s own destination, since it isn’t automatically inherited from dev.

One honest gap, kept simple: this Skill is never invoked from SAC in this series, not tried, since Joule isn’t enabled in the SAC system this build has access to. SAP’s own docs list Work Zone, S/4HANA, and SuccessFactors as the surfaces Skills reach; SAC isn’t on that list, and nothing found anywhere (SAP docs or community blogs) shows a custom Skill being invoked from SAC. Doesn’t rule it out, but as of today, this option is documented as reaching Work Zone, S/4HANA, and SuccessFactors, not SAC.

One finding while generating the OpenAPI JSON for action: FastAPI generates OpenAPI 3.1 by default; SAP Build's Action importer expects 3.0. Relabeling the version in the FastAPI constructor doesn't fix it: 3.1 and 3.0 describe nullable fields differently, so the schema actually needs rewriting, not renaming:

import json

def convert_31_to_30(spec):
    """Converts an OpenAPI 3.1 spec (FastAPI's default) to 3.0 format."""
    spec = json.loads(json.dumps(spec))  # deep copy
    spec["openapi"] = "3.0.3"

    def fix_schema(schema):
        if isinstance(schema, dict):
            if isinstance(schema.get("type"), list) and "null" in schema["type"]:
                remaining = [t for t in schema["type"] if t != "null"]
                schema["type"] = remaining[0] if len(remaining) == 1 else remaining
                schema["nullable"] = True
            for v in schema.values():
                fix_schema(v)
        elif isinstance(schema, list):
            for item in schema:
                fix_schema(item)

    fix_schema(spec.get("components", {}).get("schemas", {}))
    fix_schema(spec.get("paths", {}))
    return spec


if __name__ == "__main__":
    with open("capstone_openapi.json") as f:
        spec = json.load(f)

    converted = convert_31_to_30(spec)

    with open("openapi_v30.json", "w") as f:
        json.dump(converted, f, indent=2)

    print("Converted. New version:", converted["openapi"])

Security model: access is gated through SAP's Identity Authentication Service: a specific user group, with the Skill's environment restricted to that group. Anyone outside it gets a generic fallback response, not an error, so the restriction fails gracefully rather than leaking that the Skill exists at all.

 

Option 2: Embedded, a custom SAC widget
The experience: a planner opens a SAC story already filtered to a single project. A widget embedded in that story lets them trigger the prediction with one click: the recommended spread and its narrative explanation appear inline, no leaving SAC, no separate tool. A second action uses that spread to calculate the actual forecast, then writes the result into the plan, turning the AI's recommendation into real plan data other reports and stories can consume.

Building the widget
The widget is a SAC custom widget: a manifest declaring what it exposes to story script, and a web component implementing the actual behaviour. Here's the manifest file:

{
	"id": "com.capstone.rptbox",
	"version": "1.0.0",
	"name": "RPT Prediction",
	"description": "Calls the forecast re-spread API for a study",
	"newInstancePrefix": "RptBox",
	"icon": "",
	"vendor": "Capstone POC",
	"eula": "",
	"license": "",
	"webcomponents": [
		{
			"kind": "main",
			"tag": "com-capstone-rptbox",
			"url": "/main.js",
			"integrity": "",
			"ignoreIntegrity": true
		}
	],
	"properties": {
		"studyId": { "type": "string", "description": "Study to predict for", "default": "" },
		"narrative": { "type": "string", "description": "Plain-English explanation", "default": "" },
		"escalate": { "type": "boolean", "description": "Needs human review", "default": false },
		"derivedMilestone": { "type": "string", "description": "Milestone derived as residual", "default": "" },
		"mostConfidentMilestone": { "type": "string", "description": "Milestone with narrowest interval", "default": "" },
		"finalPercentages": { "type": "string", "description": "Percentages as JSON string", "default": "{}" },
		"status": { "type": "string", "description": "idle, loading, success or error", "default": "idle" },
		"lastError": { "type": "string", "description": "Error message if call failed", "default": "" }
	},
	"methods": {

		"getStudyId": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the study ID." },
		"invokePrediction": { "description": "Calls the backend for the current study ID." },
		"getNarrative": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the narrative." },
		"getEscalate": { "returnType": "boolean", "description": "Returns whether review is needed." },
		"getDerivedMilestone": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the derived milestone." },
		"getMostConfidentMilestone": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the most confident milestone." },
		"getFinalPercentages": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns percentages as a JSON string." },
		"getStatus": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the current status." },
		"getLastError": { "returnType": "string", "description": "Returns the last error message." }
	},
	"events": {
		"onPredictionComplete": { "description": "Called when the prediction succeeds." },
		"onPredictionError": { "description": "Called when the prediction fails." }
	}
}

Web component file:

(function () {
  let template = document.createElement("template");
  template.innerHTML = `
		<style>
		:host { display: block; font-family: sans-serif; }
		.wrap { padding: 12px; }
		.status { font-weight: bold; margin-bottom: 8px; }
		.status.error { color: #d32f2f; }
		.narrative { white-space: pre-wrap; font-size: 13px; }
		</style>
		<div class="wrap">
			<div class="status" id="status"></div>
			<div class="narrative" id="narrative"></div>
		</div>
	`;

  class RptBox extends HTMLElement {
    constructor() {
      super();
      let shadowRoot = this.attachShadow({ mode: "open" });
      shadowRoot.appendChild(template.content.cloneNode(true));
      this._shadowRoot = shadowRoot;

      // Single internal source of truth for every property.
      // All getters/setters and invokePrediction read/write these directly —
      // never through the SAC-managed property layer — so nothing depends
      // on the framework's deferred batch/render cycle.
      this._state = {
        studyId: "", narrative: "", escalate: false, derivedMilestone: "",
        mostConfidentMilestone: "", finalPercentages: "{}", status: "idle", lastError: ""
      };
    }

    onCustomWidgetBeforeUpdate(changedProperties) {
      this._state = { ...this._state, ...changedProperties };
    }

    onCustomWidgetAfterUpdate(changedProperties) {
      this._render();
    }

    setStudyId(newStudyId) {
      this._state.studyId = newStudyId;
      this._render();
      this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("propertiesChanged", {
        detail: { properties: { studyId: newStudyId } }
      }));
    }

    getStudyId() {
      return this._state.studyId;
    }

    async invokePrediction() {
      const studyId = this._state.studyId;
      if (!studyId) {
        this._fail("No study ID set. Call setStudyId() before invokePrediction().");
        return;
      }

      this._push({ status: "loading", lastError: "" });

      const BASE_URL = "https://capstone-respread-api.cfapps.us10-001.hana.ondemand.com";
      const API_KEY = "[REDACTED]";

      try {
        const response = await fetch(
          BASE_URL + "/predict-spread/" + encodeURIComponent(studyId),
          { headers: { "X-Api-Key": API_KEY } }
        );

        if (!response.ok) {
          const body = await response.text();
          throw new Error("API returned " + response.status + ": " + body);
        }

        const data = await response.json();

        this._push({
          narrative: data.narrative,
          escalate: data.escalate,
          derivedMilestone: data.derived_milestone,
          mostConfidentMilestone: data.most_confident_milestone,
          finalPercentages: JSON.stringify(data.final_percentages),
          status: "success"
        });

        this.dispatchEvent(new Event("onPredictionComplete"));
      } catch (err) {
        this._fail(err.message);
      }
    }

    _fail(message) {
      this._push({ status: "error", lastError: message });
      this.dispatchEvent(new Event("onPredictionError"));
    }

    _push(props) {
      this._state = { ...this._state, ...props };
      this._render();
      this.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("propertiesChanged", { detail: { properties: props } }));
    }

    getNarrative() { return this._state.narrative; }
    getEscalate() { return this._state.escalate; }
    getDerivedMilestone() { return this._state.derivedMilestone; }
    getMostConfidentMilestone() { return this._state.mostConfidentMilestone; }
    getFinalPercentages() { return this._state.finalPercentages; }
    getStatus() { return this._state.status; }
    getLastError() { return this._state.lastError; }

    _render() {
      const p = this._state;
      const statusEl = this._shadowRoot.getElementById("status");
      const narrativeEl = this._shadowRoot.getElementById("narrative");
      if (!statusEl || !narrativeEl) return;

      let header;
      if (p.status === "loading") {
        header = "Loading prediction...";
      } else if (p.status === "error") {
        header = "Error: " + (p.lastError || "");
      } else if (p.status === "success") {
        header = p.escalate ? "\u26A0 Needs review before submitting." : "\u2713 Ready to submit.";
      } else {
        header = "Ready. Study: " + (p.studyId || "(none set)");
      }

      statusEl.textContent = header;
      statusEl.className = "status" + (p.status === "error" ? " error" : "");
      narrativeEl.textContent = (p.status === "error") ? "" : (p.narrative || "");
    }
  }

  customElements.define("com-capstone-rptbox", RptBox);
})();
  • _state is the single source of truth. Every getter, setter, and invokePrediction read/write it directly, never through SAC's managed property layer.
  • The constructor builds a shadow DOM once, attaching the template's markup inside attachShadow({ mode: "open" }), keeps the widget's internal styling isolated from the rest of the story.
  • onCustomWidgetBeforeUpdate merges any externally-set properties (e.g. studyId bound to a filter elsewhere in the story) into _state, so there's still only one source of truth even when SAC pushes changes in from outside.
  • onCustomWidgetAfterUpdate just calls _render(): SAC's own update cycle triggers a redraw, but doesn't write to state directly.
  • setStudyId updates _state, redraws, and fires propertiesChanged, the same pattern _push() uses later, done manually here since it's a plain setter, not part of the async prediction flow.
  • invokePrediction guards against an empty studyId first, sets status to "loading", fetches the backend with the X-Api-Key header, and maps the response fields into _state on success, or routes to _fail() on any error, including a non-OK HTTP response.
  • _fail() is the one path both a missing studyId and a failed fetch funnel through: sets status to "error", stores the message, and fires onPredictionError.
  • _push() updates _state and fires propertiesChanged, so anything bound to these properties in the story picks up the change too.
  • _render() produces the "Needs review" vs. "Ready to submit" text, the actual mechanism behind the safeguard described further down.

One honest gap: the API key sits in plain text in the widget's client-side JavaScript, visible to anyone who opens dev tools, unlike a key sitting server-side. Fine for a POC, not for anything that ships. Production fix and why: covered in the final post on what changes for enterprise.

Writing the result back into the plan
This is where the widget stops being read-only. Once a prediction comes back from the backend, the widget's onPredictionComplete event fires, and the story script bound to that event pushes the five percentages into the actual planning table using SAC's setUserInput and submitData APIs.

The response comes back as a JSON string that has to be parsed and converted before it can be written anywhere:

var lists = percents.split('":');
var prior_fpe = lists[1].substring(0, lists[1].indexOf(","));
var fpe_lpi   = lists[2].substring(0, lists[2].indexOf(","));
var lpi_lplv  = lists[3].substring(0, lists[3].indexOf(","));
var lplv_csr  = lists[4].substring(0, lists[4].indexOf(","));
var post_csr  = lists[5].substring(0, lists[5].length - 1);

// The Spread measure in this model is stored as a decimal fraction (0.372), not a
// whole-number percent (37.2) — matches how the existing RateCard values are stored.
prior_fpe = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(prior_fpe) / 100));
fpe_lpi   = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(fpe_lpi)   / 100));
lpi_lplv  = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(lpi_lplv)  / 100));
lplv_csr  = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(lplv_csr)  / 100));
post_csr  = ConvertUtils.numberToString((ConvertUtils.stringToNumber(post_csr)  / 100));

var prior_fpe_sel = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "Prior FPE" };
var fpe_lpi_sel   = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "FPE to LPI" };
var lpi_lplv_sel  = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "LPI to LPLV" };
var lplv_csr_sel  = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "LPLV to CSR" };
var post_csr_sel  = { Datasource: "RPT Prediction", Milestones: "Post CSR" };

tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(prior_fpe_sel, prior_fpe);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(fpe_lpi_sel, fpe_lpi);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(lpi_lplv_sel, lpi_lplv);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(lplv_csr_sel, lplv_csr);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().setUserInput(post_csr_sel, post_csr);
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getPlanning().submitData();
tbl_rpt_vs_rc.getDataSource().refreshData();

 

Option 3: Proactive, a scheduled notification
The experience: every night, any newly created project gets automatically evaluated. The responsible manager gets a notification the next morning with the status and narrative already waiting; no one has to remember to ask, and no one has to click anything to get it started.

This runs as a scheduled SAC Application, whose script fires in onInitialization event, reusing the exact same RptBox widget from Option 2 above rather than making a fresh HTTP call to the backend.

var new_proj = tbl_new_projects.getDataSource().getResultSet();
console.log(new_proj);
var pms = ArrayUtils.create(Type.string);
var proj_ids = ArrayUtils.create(Type.string);
var email_title = "";
var i = 0;
var j = 0;

// Getting the unique list of project managers
for (i = 0; i < new_proj.length; i++) {
    if (!pms.includes(new_proj[i]["StudyID.ProjectManager"].id)) {
        pms.push(new_proj[i]["StudyID.ProjectManager"].id);
    }
}

// Batch processing the project IDs for each project manager
for (j = 0; j < pms.length; j++) {
    proj_ids.splice(0);
    for (i = 0; i < new_proj.length; i++) {
        if (new_proj[i]["StudyID.ProjectManager"].id === pms[j]) {
            proj_ids.push(new_proj[i]["StudyID"].id);
        }
    }

    // Passing a single project ID, since the backend SQL view and APIs are
    // designed to handle only one predict row at a time for this POC. In a
    // production scenario, rather than calling the RPT API in a loop, it's
    // best to update the API to accept multiple project IDs and predict
    // everything in one call, for each project manager.
    RPT_JOB.setStudyId(proj_ids[0]);
    RPT_JOB.invokePrediction();

    if (RPT_JOB.getStatus() === "success") {
        if (RPT_JOB.getEscalate()) {
            email_title = "Project Spread Prediction Results - Manual Review required";
        } else {
            if (utils.submitPredictionData(RPT_JOB.getFinalPercentages())) {
                // Returns true if the prediction was applied successfully to the forecast.
                email_title = "Project Spread Prediction Results";
            } else {
                email_title = "Project Spread Prediction Results - Not applied to the forecast";
            }
        }

        Application.sendNotification({
            title: email_title,
            content: RPT_JOB.getNarrative(),
            receivers: [pms[j]],
            isSendEmail: true,
            isSendMobileNotification: true
        });
    }
}
  • Pulls the new-project list. tbl_new_projects.getDataSource().getResultSet() reads from a table already scoped to newly created projects; this script doesn't do that filtering itself.
  • Dedupes down to project managers. One unique list of PM IDs from however many new projects showed up overnight.
  • Groups projects per manager, then predicts in one call. For each PM, it collects every new project ID belonging to them, and calls the prediction API on proj_ids[]
  • Three-state email title. Escalated (needs review), applied cleanly, or applied but write-back failed, not just success/fail.
  • One notification, two channels. Email and mobile push in the same call, using the widget's getNarrative() directly, no separate composition step.

Worth being upfront about the scenario this fits. This approach was built for a simple case: each project manager gets one or two new projects at a time, not a flood. It works well there, but it's not the shape you'd want at real volume.

For a high-volume scenario, a different architecture makes more sense. Rather than a SAC script looping through predictions one project at a time, the trigger would move upstream to Datasphere: a process there would call the prediction pipeline and write the results directly into the SAC Planning model's tables, including an attribute marking whether each project is escalated or not. A Data Action in SAC would then apply the predicted percentages based on that escalation attribute, only pushing the clean, non-escalated results into the plan. The scheduled SAC Application's job shrinks down to just one thing at that point: sending an email with a PDF export summarizing what got forecast and what got escalated, rather than driving the whole prediction loop itself.

What's next

Part 6 covers what's next: how this pipeline could actually be backtested against real outcomes, and what would need to change to take it from proof of concept to something a real enterprise could run on.

entry.title: SAP AI Core vs. SAP Build: Why You Need Both for True Enterprise AI
entry.content:
When embarking on a digital transformation journey, it is easy to look at the robust capabilities of SAP Build and wonder: "If I can develop applications, automate processes, and integrate business logic here, why do I need SAP AI Core?"

It is a fair question. SAP Build is an incredible low-code/no-code platform that empowers teams to create applications rapidly. However, when it comes to scaling, securing, and orchestrating complex artificial intelligence, SAP AI Core is the essential engine running under the hood.

Here is a look at why SAP AI Core is indispensable, even when you can handle your primary development within SAP Build.

Understanding the Roles: The Engine vs. The Body

To understand why both are necessary, it helps to use an automotive analogy:

  • SAP Build is the car’s body, dashboard, and controls. It is what the user interacts with. It defines how the application behaves, how data flows, and how the user experiences the solution.
  • SAP AI Core is the high-performance engine. It handles the heavy lifting, complex computations, model management, and secure processing of AI workloads.

While you can build the interface and logic in SAP Build, you need SAP AI Core to power the advanced AI capabilities safely and efficiently.

3 Reasons Why SAP Build Needs SAP AI Core

1. Enterprise-Grade Trust and the Generative AI Hub

While you can connect SAP Build to external APIs, doing so directly with public AI models poses significant data privacy and security risks.

  • SAP AI Core hosts the Generative AI Hub, which acts as a secure gateway to leading large language models (LLMs).
  • It ensures your enterprise data remains strictly confidential, preventing sensitive business information from being used to train public models.
  • By routing your AI requests through SAP AI Core, you get built-in safety guards, data masking, and compliance out of the box—security features that SAP Build can consume but cannot generate on its own.
2. Heavy-Duty Model Lifecycle Management

If your development requires custom machine learning models, SAP Build is not designed to train or deploy them.

  • SAP AI Core is built to handle GPU-intensive workloads, execute training pipelines, and serve custom models at scale.
  • It manages the entire AI lifecycle, allowing you to monitor model performance, retrain models as business data changes, and manage version control seamlessly.
3. Cost Optimization and Resource Scheduling

Running AI models—especially deep learning or large language models—can be incredibly resource-intensive.

  • SAP AI Core optimizes infrastructure costs by scheduling resources dynamically. It spins up compute power when a model needs to run and scales it down when idle.
  • Attempting to manage these compute resources directly within an application layer like SAP Build would lead to inefficiencies and unpredictable costs.

The Perfect Synergy: Better Together

The goal is not to choose between SAP AI Core and SAP Build, but to leverage them together:

  1. Deploy with AI Core: Your data scientists and developers use SAP AI Core to securely deploy, manage, and access powerful AI models and LLMs.
  2. Deliver with Build: Your application developers use SAP Build to quickly create the user interface, trigger the AI workflows, and present the insights to business users.

By combining the rapid development speed of SAP Build with the robust, secure AI infrastructure of SAP AI Core, you get the best of both worlds: maximum agility without compromising on security, scalability, or control.

This blog outlines how Maintenance and Operations Teams can leverage a conversational SAP Joule Agent to seamlessly retrieve Asset Health Alerts from SAP Asset Performance Management(APM) and their associated S/4HANA Maintenance Notifications by using Low-Code and No-Code approach.

If you would like to gain a deeper understanding of SAP Joule Skill and Agent, check out my latest SAP blog posts below, where I have shared my hands-on journey of building SAP Joule Skills and Agents using low-code and no-code approach.

  • SAP JOULE & ME : My First JOULE Skill in SAP EHSM-Incident Management Without Coding 
  • SAP JOULE Agent & ME : My First JOULE Agent in SAP EHSM-Incident Management Without Coding 

In modern Industrial plants, SAP Asset Performance Management(APM) acts as the central nervous system for asset health. SAP APM Rule Management engine constantly monitors sensors data like vibration, temperature, pressure etc., and automatically triggers Technical Object Alerts the moment an anomaly is detected. Alerts provide insights into the state of Asset Health, and help maintenance team anticipate potential failures.

By connecting SAP Asset Performance Management(APM) with a tailored SAP Joule Agent, my Maintenance program has shifted from click-heavy search process to an interactive conversation. This helps my Maintenance Team retrieve "Alerts" and S/4HANA "Maintenance Notifications" associated with the Alerts.

High Level Business Challenges:

  • Asset health alerts are generated continuously from condition monitoring Rule engine in SAP APM.
  •  Users need to navigate multiple screens to identify the "Severity", "Status" of the alert.
  • Critical Alerts may not receive Immediate attention.
  • Maintenance Team lacks consolidated view of Maintenance Notifications status with respect to Alerts.

Solution Overview:

To achieve this I used the following "Manage Alerts" & "Manage Maintenance Notification Service" APIs.

We had better test the APIs using "POSTMAN" to have better understanding of Metadata...let us test the "Manage Alerts" & "Maintenance Notifications" APIs.

Using the above standard APIs, I have created Joule Skills below and wrapped them into an Joule Agent.

 

 

Once Joule Agent setup is done and tested, we can "Release" and "Deploy" in the designated environment.

Finding Associated Maintenance Notifications:
