entry.title: Building and Consuming an MCP Server in SAP Integration Suite - Connecting it to Claude and Joule
entry.content:
Introduction

In this blog, I want to share my hands-on experience of building an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server in SAP Integration Suite, and then consuming it from two different AI agents - Claude and Joule. I explored this end-to-end, from the initial setup and configuration challenges to the final working agents, and I am documenting the journey here in case it helps others attempting the same thing.

Prerequisites

Before you start creating API and MCP artifacts in Integration Suite, make sure the following are in place:

  1. Cloud Integration and API Management capabilities are activated in Integration Suite.
  2. The Integration Cell runtime is enabled - go to Settings → Runtimes and confirm it shows Active. The MCP Server artifact runs on Integration Cell, it cannot be deployed to the classic Cloud Integration runtime.
  3. Your service plan is Premium or Enhanced edition - MCP is available only in the Premium and Enhanced edition plans
  4. The PI_Integration_Developer role collection is assigned to your user in the BTP Cockpit.

Architecture

Here's the high-level flow I used to connect Claude and Joule to Integration Suite via the MCP server:

                Joule / Claude
                      |
   Claude Connector / Joule Destination
   (connection via Developer Hub or BTP OAuth credentials)
                      |
               MCP Server artifact
                      |
           (accesses API artifacts)
                      |
  API Artifact (Integration Suite OData APIs /
                    CPI iFlows)
                      |
               API response
                      |
            Back to Claude / Joule

I have split this blog into two parts. first, creating the MCP server in Integration Suite, and second, connecting it separately to Claude and to Joule. The MCP server itself stays the same in both scenarios, only the connection method changes.

For the examples in this blog, I used two inputs to build the API specification, the standard Integration Suite OData APIs, and a plain iFlow consumed through the MCP server.

Part 1: Creating the MCP Server in Integration Suite

Step 1: Creating the API Artifact

An MCP artifact can be created in a couple of ways in Integration Suite:

  • Option 1: Create an API artifact by uploading an OpenAPI 3.0 specification, then deploy it to the Integration Cell runtime.
  • Option 2: Configure the target URL directly and build the API specification inside the MCP artifact itself.

I went with Option 1, using the standard Integration Suite OData API as my example.

 

 

1.1 Creating the API Artifact

In an Integration Suite package, I created an API artifact with the Runtime profile set to Integration Cell.

 

 

Under Select API type, I chose URL or Specification, and within that, OData - since the MCP server was going to consume a standard Integration Suite OData service. There are other options too: REST (useful for posting data to an iFlow or a third-party API) and SOAP, if SOAP services are involved.

 

 

 

 

Note: Use OData if your API artifact relies purely on OData APIs. If it's a mix of OData and iFlow calls, go with REST instead - OData can still be reached via the HTTP adapter within a REST based API artifact.

The next important step is preparing the API specification to upload into the API artifact. I used the YAML file from the SAP Business Accelerator Hub to generate my API specification.

 

 

 
Note: The JSON/YAML file from SAP Business Accelerator Hub is in Swagger 2.0 format, but the MCP server expects the specification in OpenAPI 3.0. You can convert it using an online tool - I used the Swagger Editor and its converter  or alternatively, use the API artifact's "create" option to generate a spec from prompts.

 

 
Once the spec was uploaded with the endpoint details, I validated it inside the API artifact. The spec I used contained the standard CPI OData APIs.

 

 

 
From there, I navigated to the Policy section and configured the OData adapter with the required credentials deployed in the security material, everything else stayed unchanged. Under Authentication, the api.invoke scope is present by default, but you can add your own scope if needed. Make sure Trust Upstream MCP Authorization is enabled.
 
 

 

 
I then deployed the API artifact after completing this configuration.

 

Step 2: Creating the MCP Server

With the API artifact deployed, I created the MCP server on top of it.

 

 

I selected the MCP artifact and chose API as the Source type, since I already had an API artifact created. (There's also an HTTP endpoint option if you want to bypass the API artifact step entirely.)

 

 
Under Provide MCP details, I selected the API artifact I had created and provided a unique path under MCP path.

 

 

 

Once created, the MCP server picks up the tools from the API artifact, I made sure all tools were available in the MCP artifact.

 

  

Important configuration step: under the MCP artifact's Policy, the authentication parameter is OAuth with Client Certificate (not modifiable). In the Authorization policy setting, you choose between:

  • OAuth scope — for connecting the MCP server using BTP integration flow credentials.
  • Developer key — for connecting the MCP server using Developer Hub credentials.

 

 
The HTTP adapter configuration didn't need any changes - it still points to the API artifact I created.
 
 
I deployed the MCP artifact and confirmed its status under Manage Integration Content, in the Integration Cell runtime.
 
With that, the MCP server itself was ready. The next steps cover how I connected this MCP server to Claude, and separately, to Joule.

 

Part 2: Connecting the MCP Server to Claude

Claude uses a redirect mechanism to connect to an MCP server, so the traditional BTP OAuth credentials alone aren't sufficient here. I used the Developer Hub method instead to connect the MCP server to Claude.

Steps I followed

  1. In the Developer Hub, under Admin Center, I navigated to Content.

 

           
 
        2. I clicked on Business System, where all the deployed API and MCP servers are listed.
 
              

              

 

              

 

         3. I selected the required MCP server and created a Product from it.

 

 

              

 

               

        4. I navigated to the newly created product and created a new Subscription for it.

 

               
 
         5. I provided a name and short text for the agent. The key part here is configuring the Claude URL in the Callback URL field -                 this is what allows Claude to authenticate against the MCP server.

 

 
                

 

Once the agent was created, I could see the Token URL along with the ID and Secret.

 

 
Adding the CPI MCP server to Claude
  1. In Claude, I navigated to Customize → Connectors → Add Custom Connector.    

 

            

        2. I provided a name and the MCP server URL (from Integration Suite), then clicked Continue.

 

              
 
          3. Under Authentication, I selected Always Required, and under OAuth Client, I chose Use your own OAuth client, then clicked                Add.

 

                
 
Once authentication succeeded, all the tools inside the MCP server became visible in Claude. By default, tools show as Needs Approval - I changed the status to Approved for the tools I wanted to test and use (you can also approve all of them at once).

 

 

 

I have shared a few results below from testing this in Claude - the responses were genuinely impressive.

 

 

 

Part 3: Connecting the MCP Server to Joule

I connected Joule to CPI in two different ways:

  1. By creating a Skill and Action that uses a CPI iFlow to make the required API calls and respond to Joule (essentially, straightforward iFlow execution).
  2. By consuming the CPI MCP server directly inside a Joule agent, providing instructions and an LLM model, and then deploying it to an environment.

Here is how I connected the CPI MCP server to Joule using the second approach:

  1. For Claude, I used the Developer Hub method — but for Joule, I used BTP OAuth credentials (the integration flow credentials, not the API ones). In the BTP Cockpit, I navigated to my Build subaccount, then Connectivity → Destinations, and created a destination with only the host name — no path prefix, since that gets provided inside the Joule agent itself. I configured the destination with OAuth details, and added these additional properties:
    • sap-joule-studio-mcp-server = true
    • sap.processautomation.enabled = true
    • sap.mcp.tools.enabled = true
  2. I repeated the same setup in the Joule subaccount.
    Note: The destination must exist in both subaccounts, with the same name and the same properties.
  3. For each destination, in both subaccounts, I clicked Check Connection to confirm it was healthy.
  4. Once the destination was created, I went to SAP Build → Control Tower → Destination and confirmed it was available there too.

     

     

  5. Next, I created an agent in Joule to consume the CPI MCP server. In the Build lobby, I clicked Create and selected Joule Skill/Agent.

     

  6. I provided a name and description to proceed, and once the project was created, clicked Create again to build the Joule agent itself.
 
 

 

              

 

              
 
         7. I provided a name, identifier, and description. (Worth noting: Joule uses every detail you provide here when executing a task,               so it's worth being thorough.)

 

 
               
 
          8. Inside the Joule agent, I provided the Expertise and Instructions in detail, so the agent would behave correctly based on my                prompts, and selected the model settings to fit my needs.

 

                
                
 
            9. Under MCP servers, I clicked Add MCP server, gave it a unique name and description, and under the Advanced tab,                                provided the MCP server path (the same Integration Cell host name used in the destination) and selected the destination I                  had created.

 

 
                        
 
               10. After adding it, I clicked Refresh Tools, which pulled in and displayed all the tools available inside the MCP server.

 

 
                      
 
As a final step, I set the agent output format to Markdown so Joule could render the output cleanly. Once everything was configured, I saved the agent and deployed it to an environment (environments can be created under Control Tower → Environment). Additional tools can be added to this agent if required
 
 
With that, the MCP server was live and usable from both Claude and Joule. Provided the Joule results in Business use case section

Business Use Cases I Built With This

1. CPI Monitoring Agent

As shown throughout this blog, this agent uses the standard Integration Suite OData APIs to pull monitoring information based on user queries. I have handed this over to the support team and business admins so they can retrieve monitoring information and perform a few admin tasks directly, without needing to log into Integration Suite.

2. SuccessFactors Agent

I am currently working on an ongoing SuccessFactors implementation project that integrates with multiple systems - Concur, Active Directory, SAP, Staffbase, and others. As the project entered the SIT phase, the functional team needed support from the CPI team to run ad-hoc flows. I built this agent so the functional team could run the entire testing process from Joule itself, without involving the CPI team each time.

For example: the user tells Joule which interface they want to run, and Joule suggests the required inputs (filter type and value). Once the user provides that input, an API call goes to the CPI iFlow, which executes the transaction, fetches the monitoring report based on the correlation ID, and returns the monitoring status directly in Joule - completing the whole loop.

 

 

 

What I found elegant about this agent is that the inputs can be very user-friendly. Users only need to specify the interface and filter type they want, for instance, entering a date like "25th Aug" for a last-modified-date filter and the API specification takes care of formatting it correctly.

3. IDoc Reprocessing Agent

This agent works from both Claude and Joule. The user provides a date range, and the agent retrieves IDoc failures from SAP (via WE02) through an OData call routed through the MCP server. (By default, the OData request attempts to reprocess the IDoc in SAP first — only IDocs that still fail after reprocessing show up as failures in CPI.) For genuine failures, the agent creates a ServiceNow request and reports everything back to the user.

Challenges I Faced

  1. Connecting the CPI MCP server to Claude — in my initial attempts, the redirect URL wasn't configured, and it wasn't clear how to do it. I eventually got Claude's redirect URL and configured it in the Developer Hub.
  2. Setting up authentication via Developer Hub — the full configuration process wasn't clear at first, and took some trial and error to get right.
  3. Choosing the right authorization policy inside the MCP artifact — for Joule versus Claude. The api.invoke role is meant for Developer Hub credentials, while ESBMessaging.send (or any custom role) works for BTP OAuth credentials. To use BTP OAuth, you need to select the OAuth scope or developer key option under Authorization Type.
  4. Defining the API specification — for the CPI agent, I used the standard Integration Suite OData JSON/YAML files, which come in Swagger 2.0 by default, while the API artifact expects OpenAPI 3.0. Getting the conversion and customization right took some care.
  5. Handling multiple target URLs for the SuccessFactors agent — I needed to call a CPI iFlow for posting data, and OData APIs for fetching monitoring logs, which meant defining two target URLs in the API specification. I solved this inside the API artifact policy using a router. The tricky part was figuring out what payload was coming into the iFlow, since there's no built-in trace option — I ended up using debug mode and found the API path coming through in the header, which I then used to route to the correct URL.
  6. Getting the Joule destination right — the host name of the MCP server (Integration Cell) needs to be provided during destination creation, along with the OAuth credentials, and the three additional properties (sap-joule-studio-mcp-server, sap.processautomation.enabled, sap.mcp.tools.enabled) all need to be set to true.

Claude vs. Joule: What I Learned

To be clear, this isn't a comparison of which tool is better,  it's about how each one needs to be configured and used:

  • Joule works more precisely the more detailed instructions you give it while building the agent. Requests from Joule don't go directly against the MCP server's API specification, Joule first checks the instructions you defined, and acts accordingly. Claude, on the other hand, works directly against the API specification and responds based on that.
  • Joule expects a much more detailed API specification. For example, if you want to fetch a monitoring status, you need to explicitly define in the HTTP 200 response how the data should be extracted. Claude doesn't need this level of detail, it's able to understand the response and extract the relevant output on its own.

Joule is always the first choice as it is within the SAP ecosystem, and I am hopeful that Joule Studio 2.0 will bring more capabilities to close this gap further.

Conclusion

That's a summary of how I built an MCP server in SAP Integration Suite and connected it to both Claude and Joule. I hope this is useful to others exploring the same setup, happy to hear feedback, suggestions, or answer any questions in the comments.

entry.title: Leveraging Joule Studio for SAP SuccessFactors
entry.content:
I'm excited to share my first blog, based on my learnings and experience working with Joule Studio. @amrutha_g will be the co-author of this blog.

This blog introduces Joule Studio and demonstrates how SAP SuccessFactors users can create tailored conversational experiences using Actions, Skills, and Agents. Through a practical illustration, readers will learn how to build, test, and deploy AI-powered capabilities that enable users to extract business information by communication through natural language.

  1. Introduction to Joule Studio 
  2. Key Features of Joule Studio 
  3. Prerequisites  
  4. Understanding the Three Building Blocks of Joule Studio 
  5. Action Editor Overview 
  6. Skill Editor Deep Dive 
  7. Agent Editor Overview 
  8. Testing Skills and Agents 
  9. Conclusion

Introduction

Joule Studio is an important component of SAP Build; it's a comprehensive suite of low-code and no-code solutions designed to enhance application development and leverage the power of generative AI.

It let’s us expand Joule's capabilities and knowledge to meet the distinct requirements of the organization.

With Joule embedded in SAP SuccessFactors, Joule Studio serves as a workspace to create and deploy custom capabilities. These can in turn be used within our instance to perform informational/ transactional operations with the help of prompts in human language.

Features

  • Develop new skills for Joule that enable it to perform additional, custom, and pre-determined tasks that supports business processes.
  • Design interactive Joule agents that collaborate with Joule to tackle complex or multi-step tasks efficiently.
  • Manage and deploy advanced versions of skills and Joule agents to promote ongoing enhancements and flexibility.

Let us consider a scenario to understand more:

A user has an Employee ID. Using that, they want to fetch the first name and last name of the employee. Instead of navigating around the SuccessFactors UI and searching for an Employee, the user would like to simply ask Joule.

Prerequisites

  • An active user (developer) license is required to build, test, and deploy your custom Joule skills.
  • Joule should be enabled in the SuccessFactors instance

Building Blocks of Joule Studio

There are mainly 3 - building blocks of Joule Studio:

  1. Actions: An action is SAP's building block that wraps a single API call (or endpoint) - defining its inputs and outputs — so that it can be securely exposed and reused inside a Joule Skill or Agent.
  2. Skills: A skill is part of an advanced AI model and can act on specific operations by leveraging the content of the conversation. It helps in combining various Actions together
  3. Agents: A Joule agent is an independent, multipurpose-tool system that solves complex problems by selecting and executing appropriate tools dynamically. It helps combine various skills together.

Creating any of the above blocks requires a project. A project serves as a comprehensive workspace where we can create and manage various skills and agents related to a particular use case.

Before proceeding, start by creating a new project in Joule Studio.

Refer this Create a Project in Joule Studio, classic edition | SAP Help Portal to create a project.

Action Editor

The Action Editor is the workspace where we can create, modify, and manage actions.

The action editor makes API operations available to actions while also simplifying input and output values. We can also use the editor to test the operation of an action. To obtain reusable action artifacts, release and publish the Actions project to the library.

For this scenario, we would be using the Get Entities from User API

The image below illustrates the Action Editor.

The Actions pane consists of a complete list of all the API actions related to the project.

For each API, we have three tabs available: Input, Output and Test.

  • The Input tab is used to define the parameters required by the API to retrieve the desired data. These input parameters are passed to the API during execution and determine the results returned by the API.

Following are the fields available in the Input tab can be used to customize and refine the output returned by the API call.

  • $top: Specifies the maximum number of records to retrieve. By default, all available records are returned.
  • $skip: Specifies the number of records to skip before returning the results.
  • $count: Returns the total number of records that match the query criteria.
  • $filter: Applies conditions to filter the results based on specific field values.
  • $search: Searches for records that match the specified search value.
  • $orderby: Sorts the results based on one or more selected fields.

For our case, we have added the below condition to the $filter tab. ‘userId’ is the corresponding field for the employee ID.

To know more about the API’s and their fields definitions, you can refer to the SAP documentation below:
About SAP SuccessFactors APIs | SAP Help Portal

  • The Output tab consists of two sections: Header and Body. The Body section displays the fields which would be returned by the API call. Here, we can add or remove fields as needed to customize the output according to the requirements. For our scenario, we have retained the fields below and removed the rest.

  • The Test tab is used to validate and test the API using sample input values before using it into actual skill. It helps ensure that the API returns the expected results and allows us to refine the query parameters as needed. Provide the employee ID in $search field and try testing the API

For more information about the Action Editor, refer to below document from SAP:
Overview of an Action Editor | SAP Help Portal

Skill Editor

The Skill Editor is the workspace used to create, modify, and manage skills in Joule Studio.

Skills can be built using any of the following Activities:

  1. Action: Use one or more actions that have been created and incorporate them into the skill workflow.
  2. Process: Configure the skill to invoke a process created in SAP Build Process Automation.
  3. Automation: Configure the skill to trigger an automation built using SAP Build Process Automation.
  4. Skill: Reuse an existing Joule skill by incorporating it into another skill.
  5. Condition: Add decision-making logic to the skill by defining conditions that control the workflow based on specific criteria.

For more information about the activities, refer here: Add Activities to the Skill | SAP Help Portal

In the example shown below, a skill - EmployeeDetails has been created by incorporating an Action into the skill workflow.

The Trigger tab is where we define the basic details of a skill, including its Name, Identifier, and Description. The Identifier is automatically generated and pre-populated by the system.

The Description plays a significant role in aiding the Joule Assistant to understand the skill's purpose and area of specialization. This will allow Joule to identify and invoke the most relevant skill based on the user's prompt.

The Trigger tab is the place where we also define the input and output parameters for the skill.

  • Skill Inputs are variables that capture the information required from the end user. Ex: empid
  • Skill Outputs are used to store the data returned by the skill upon execution. In this case, we will define the variable of type list, so that it returns all the relevant fields.
    For our case, we will define the output of type list, so that it fetches all the relevant results returned by the API call.  

These parameters serve as the interface through which information is passed in and out of the skill.

Next, we can add an Action to the skill workflow by selecting the + icon. This is the action that was created in the previous step.

Each action consists of three tabs: General, Inputs, and Outputs.

The General tab displays the action name along with the Destination Variable. The destination variable stores the endpoint of the instance through which the information needs to be obtained. This will be created by us.

It allows the skill to access and map the action's output data to the appropriate fields, conditions, or downstream actions.

The Inputs tab is used to map the input variables defined earlier in the skill. These variables are passed to the action to ensure that the API receives the correct input values during execution.

In most cases, input variables are configured within the $filter parameter to retrieve the required data based on specific criteria.

Formulas can also be used to combine multiple input variables, aiding the creation of dynamic and more complex API queries.

In this case, the below expression has been used in the $filter tab. We have mapped userId field in the API definition to our skill Input - empid.

The Outputs tab displays the fields returned by the API call. It allows us to view the data that will be available after the action is executed and identify the output fields that can be used in subsequent steps of the skill workflow.

In the End section, map the skill's output variables to the appropriate fields returned by the action. This ensures that the relevant data retrieved from the API call is exposed as the final output of the skill and can be presented to the user or consumed by downstream processes. For this scenario, we have mapped the API result list to our output variable.

Agent Editor

Agents are created by combining one or more skills and providing detailed instructions that define how those skills should be aligned to perform a particular task.

By combining skills with proper execution logic, agents can interpret user requests, determine the relevant actions to be performed, and delivers the required outcome.

Refer to the below SAP documentation to know more about the Agent Editor

Create a Joule Agent | SAP Help Portal

For our case, we will add the 'EmployeeDetails' skill to the tool and provide instructions as below:

“When a user provides an Employee ID, invoke the EmployeeDetails skill using the supplied Employee ID as input. Retrieve the employee information from the skill response and present the results to the user in a clear and structured format. If the Employee ID is missing, prompt the user to provide it. If no employee record is found, inform the user accordingly.”

Testing the Skill/Agent

Once satisfied with the configuration of the skill or agent, select Test to validate its functionality. During testing, provide the appropriate connection details and endpoints for the SAP SuccessFactors instance to ensure successful execution and accurate results.

The image below shows the Joule Test tab.

The above image shows the testing of our skill.

Here, users can test the skill or agent by entering a prompt in natural, conversational language. Joule analyses the prompt and calls the most appropriate skill or agent to handle the request.

On entering the employee ID, Joule fetches the employee’s details from the instance.

Verify that the system correctly identifies and invokes the desired skill or agent based on the user's input. Once the execution is successful, the response is displayed in the chat interface in a clear and structured format, allowing us to validate both the behavior of the skill and the accuracy of the returned results.

After testing, deploy the project. This ensures that the Agent is ready to be used within the Joule chat in the instance.

Conclusion

The blog helps us to explore Joule Studio, and how it can be leveraged for SuccessFactors. It also explains how Actions, Skills, and Agents can contribute to building these experiences. An Action enables a specific operation, Skills help us combine actions, and Agents can help orchestrate these skills together.

With Joule Studio, the possibilities go beyond what the user can find in the application —they can also change how the user interacts with it.

entry.title: SAP Joule for Developers: End of the Promotional Period and The Path Forward
entry.content:
SAP Joule for Developers, which brought generative AI capabilities into SAP Build and ABAP at no additional cost during its initial promotional period, is ending on September 30th, 2026.  We are extending the promo offer for SAP Build features to December 31st, 2026, and this post explains exactly what that means for you, what happens to each capability you may be using today, and what your path forward looks like after December 31st, 2026. 

We know changes like this require planning, and we want to give you as much clarity as possible, well in advance, so you can make informed decisions for your team and your projects. 

What Does This Mean for You? 

If you are using SAP Build generative AI capabilities today — SAP Build Process Automation generative AI features or Joule Studio, classic edition generative AI features — you retain full access through December 31, 2026. AI chat in SAP Build Code is already rolled out in Business Application Studio and will continue beyond December 31, 2026. SAP Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities will be commercially available starting October 1, 2026, outside the promotion (previously announced here). 

SAP Build continues as a customer-managed solution development platform for extending SAP applications. What is changing is the commercial structure behind certain AI capabilities that were offered on a promotional basis, and the transition of the SAP Joule for Developers brand that will only be associated with ABAP AI capabilities as we move into 2027. 

Why Are We Making This Change? 

SAP Joule for Developers promotional period was designed to give customers hands-on experience with generative AI in SAP Build without an immediate commercial commitment. That exploration phase has provided real-world signals on what delivers value. Based on customer feedback, we made deliberate decisions for each capability.  Where usage and value are clear, we are moving capabilities into supported commercial models; where strategic alternatives exist to deliver better customer value, we are directing investment accordingly. 

What Happens to Each Capability?

ABAP AI — Continues under commercial licensing 

As announced in May 2026, ABAP AI moves to consumption-based pricing (PUPM model) effective October 1, 2026. If you are currently using ABAP AI under SAP Joule for Developers promotional access, SAP will contact you before the transition date with licensing details. More details available here. 

Action required: Plan for a licensing transition before October 1, 2026. 

AI assistance in SAP Build Code — Already Available in Business Application Studio 

AI Chat in SAP Build Code has already been rolled out in Business Application Studio (BAS) for those using build-code (SAP Build Code) or build-default (SAP Build Developer) plans. This will remain available beyond December 31, 2026. No action is required from customers; your AI coding assistance experience is uninterrupted and enhanced to now allow you to configure your own large language model provider, such as SAP AI Core, a third party LLM provider, or Github Copilot. 

SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features — Access through December 31, 2026 

SAP Build customers using generative AI features in SAP Build Process Automation — including process generation, decision generation, form generation, script generation, and summarization — can continue using those features until December 31, 2026. After December 31, 2026, you can continue using SAP Build Process Automation without generative AI support. You can begin exploring Joule Studio for a new agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

Your existing automations, processes, and decisions built in SAP Build Process Automation are unaffected. This transition impacts only the ability to use AI while authoring new content, not your existing artifacts.

Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI features — Access through December 31, 2026 

Customers using Joule Studio, classic edition can continue using its generative AI features such as agent creation and deletion, configuring agent properties, adding and removing tools, and triggering test modes until December 31, 2026. After December 31, 2026, you can continue using Joule Studio, classic edition, but without generative AI support. This specifically and only refers to the generative AI support during design time. You can begin exploring the new Joule Studio and its agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

Frequently Asked Questions 

Is SAP Build being deprecated? 

No. SAP Build continues as a customer managed application development platform for extending SAP applications, automations and digital workspaces. 

Do my existing SAP Build projects, automations, and code get affected? 

No. Your built artifacts are fully intact. Only AI-assisted authoring capabilities are affected by this transition. 

Can I keep using SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features and Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI features? 

Yes — GenAI features continue up to December 31, 2026. After this time, Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI features such as agent creation and deletion, configuring agent properties, adding and removing tools, and triggering test mode will be removed. SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features such as artifact (process, form, data type, decision) creation with natural language will be removed. These GenAI features refer specifically and only to the generative AI support during design time.

What happens after December 31, 2026 for SAP Build Process Automation GenAI and Joule Studio, classic edition GenAI? 

For SAP Build Process Automation and Joule Studio, classic edition, you can continue using these products without generative AI support after December 31, 2026. You can begin exploring Joule Studio for a new agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

What about the AI assistance in SAP Build Code? 

AI Chat is already rolled out in Business Application Studio (BAS) and continues beyond December 31, 2026. No action needed. 

Will ABAP AI Capabilities still be available after the promotional period ends? 

Yes — ABAP AI capabilities moves to the Per User Per Month (PUPM) commercial license from October 1, 2026. ABAP Development Tools remain free; only the AI capabilities require licensing. 

What should I do right now? 

If you use ABAP AI, engage your SAP account manager to plan the licensing transition before October 1, 2026. For SAP Build Process Automation GenAI and Joule Studio, classic edition, you can continue using SAP Build Process Automation and Joule Studio, classic edition without generative AI support after December 31st, 2026.  

You can begin exploring Joule Studio for a new agentic development experience once it is generally available in H2 2026. 

Who do I contact with questions? 

Your SAP account manager or Customer Success Partner. Or leave a comment below. 

 

Next Steps

  1. If you use SAP Joule for Developers, ABAP AI Capabilities — engage your SAP account manager now to plan the AI Units licensing transition before October 1, 2026. Purchase the AI Units contract (SKU 8019164) on the SAP Store. 
  2. If you use SAP Build Process Automation GenAI features or Joule Studio, classic edition genAI features, your access continues through December 31, 2026. After that date, you can continue using SAP Build Process Automation and Joule Studio, classic edition without generative AI support. You can begin exploring Joule Studio once it is generally available in H2 2026. 
  3. If you use the AI chat in SAP Build Code — no action needed. The capability continues in Business Application Studio beyond December 31, 2026 under fair use limits and is enhanced to now allow you to configure your own large language model provider, such as SAP AI Core, a third party LLM provider, or Github Copilot. 
  4. Share this post internally with developers, architects, and project owners who need to plan for these changes.

If you have questions, please leave a comment below or reach out to your SAP account manager or Customer Success Partner.

entry.title: What’s new in Mobile development kit client 26.9
entry.content:
Dear Community,

I'm happy to announce that a new release of the Mobile development kit (MDK) is now available for all SAP Build and Mobile Services customers. You can download it from the SAP Software Center, or from the community download page.

The SAP Mobile Services Client version 26.9.0 is available on Google Play and Apple App stores.

SAP MDK enables developers and technical business users to build cross-platform mobile applications. It allows you to build your application once, in an integrated development environment (Visual Studio Code / SAP Business Application Studio) and run it natively on Mobile (iOS & Android).  

The following enhancements are available only on iOS and Android platforms:

  • Supportability Enhancements
    • Support Crash Reporting
    UI Enhancements
    • Improved Sync Error Handling for Multi-User Switching
    • Display Attachment Title and File Size in Attachment Form Cell
    • Custom Search Icon Support for Text Input, List Picker, and Section Search 
    • Support Section page as Filter page
    MDK Editor Updates 
    • Automatic Dependencies Checks in MDK Editor VS Code Extension 
    • From MDK Genie to Agentic Development (Applicable in SAP Business Application Studio)

Support Crash Reporting

With this release, your MDK apps can now automatically capture and report crash data to SAP Mobile Services, giving administrators greater visibility into app stability issues in production. This enables teams to investigate crashes more efficiently.

Key Benefits

  • Faster troubleshooting: Crash logs are automatically uploaded to mobile services and provide valuable diagnostic information that can help developers and administrators investigate and resolve app crashes more efficiently.
  • User privacy and control: Crash data is uploaded only after the user has provided consent, with the consent decision stored per user and device.
  • Mobile Services controlled configuration: Administrators can enable or disable crash reporting through the mobile services admin UI without requiring changes to the app.
    Admin settings for crash log upload
  • In-app consent management:  App developers can expose crash reporting preferences in the app settings, allowing users to view or change their consent.
    Crash Report Collection Consent View
  • Improved app stability monitoring: Administrators can access crash information to better understand app stability and identify recurring issues.
    Uploaded Crash Logs page in mobile services admin UI

Client APIs: Three new client APIs allow apps to query and manage consent from within the app settings page.

  • isCrashReportingEnabled(): Returns true when crash reporting is enabled in the mobile services and app is not in demo mode.
let crashReportStatus = context.isCrashReportingEnabled();​
  • isCurrentCrashConsentAllowed(): Returns true if user has granted consent for crash reporting.
let consentAllowedStatus = context.isCurrentCrashConsentAllowed();​
  • showCrashConsentDialog(): Programmatically displays the crash reporting consent dialog. App developers should expose the crash consent screen in the app settings so users can review or change their preference. An error apperas if crash reporting is not enabled in the mobile services or when running in demo mode.
export default function CrashConsentDialog(context) {
    try {
        context.showCrashConsentDialog();
    } catch (error) {
        alert('Error showing crash consent dialog: ' + error.message);
    }
}​

For more information, refer to this documentation.

Improved Sync Error Handling for Multi-User Switching

We have improved sync error handling for multi-user scenarios, particularly when a previous user leaves unresolved business data on a shared device.
Previously, if a user made local changes, encountered a sync error, and logged off without resolving it, the next user could not continue using the app. On devices managed by MDM, where reinstalling the app may not be an option, this could leave the device unusable until the previous user returned to resolve the issue.
By default, when offline conflict handling is not configured, the only available action is Return to Sign In Screen. The previous user must sign in again and resolve the transaction issue before another user can continue using the app.
With MDK 26.9, configurable conflict handling allows the next user to resolve the previous user's pending transactions directly from the Transaction Issue screen and continue to the app without requiring the previous user to sign in again.

Key Benefits

  • Improved device availability: The next user can continue using the app even when the previous user is unavailable to resolve pending offline transactions.
  • Simplified user switching: Users can resolve or discard the previous user's pending transactions directly from the Transaction Issue screen without requiring the previous user to sign in again.
  • Administrator control: Administrators can enable offline conflict handling and select how pending transactions should be handled.
  • Data recovery option: When configured, a snapshot of the previous user's pending offline data can be uploaded before the transactions are discarded, providing an option for administrator recovery.

Configure Conflict Resolution in Mobile Services: To enable conflict resolution for multi-user mode:

  • In the Mobile Services cockpit, navigate to your application.
  • Under Shared Devices, enable Allow Upload of Pending Changes from Previous User.
  • Enable Offline Conflict Handling in Multi-User Mode.

    Admin settings to enable offline conflict handling

  • Select the desired conflict resolution mode:
    •  Discard Pending Transactions: Discards the previous user's pending transactions immediately.
    • Discard Pending Transactions After Upload: Uploads a snapshot of the previous user's offline data to the server for potential administrator recovery, and then discards the pending transactions. This requires:
      • Enable the offline store upload policy in mobile services
        Admin settings to enabel offline store upload
      • metadata changes using OfflineOptions.MultiUserConflictHandling in the .service file
//Excerpt of a .service file 
   "OfflineOptions": {
        "StoreParameters": {},
        "MultiUserConflictHandling": {
            "UploadEncryptionKey": "/MyApp/Rules/GenKey.js",
            "UploadRequestQueueOnly": true
        }
    },​

Runtime Behavior

When offline conflict handling is enabled, a conflict-handling action is displayed alongside Return to Sign In Screen on the Transaction Issue screen. When the user selects the conflict-handling action, a confirmation dialog is displayed before the selected action is applied. After the user confirms:

  • The configured conflict resolution policy is applied.
  • The app proceeds directly to the new user's main page without requiring the previous user to sign in.

If the user cancels the confirmation dialog or selects Return to Sign In Screen:

  • No conflict resolution is performed.
  • The previous user can sign in again and resolve the transaction issue manually.

 Runtime behavior on iOS and Android platforms


For more information, refer to this documentation.

Display Attachment Title and File Size in Attachment Form Cell

The MDK Attachment Form Cell now displays the attachment title (file name) and file size, making it easier for users to identify and review files before submission. This display is automatic and no metadata configuration changes are required.  Previously, users could not see the file name or size of an attachment, making it difficult to distinguish between files or understand their size.

Key Benefits

  • Improved file identification: Users can quickly distinguish between multiple attachments by their file name.
  • Better file awareness: Users can see the attachment size before submission or review.
  • Fiori UX alignment: The Attachment Form Cell experience is more consistent with standard Fiori UX expectations.

Examples displaying file name and size in FormCell attachment control

Custom Search Icon Support for Text Input, List Picker, and Section Search

MDK now supports custom icon configuration for TextInput (SimpleProperty), ListPicker, and Section controls, allowing app developers to replace default icons with custom images and provide a more tailored app experience.

All supported icon properties can reference metadata image paths, resource images, SAP icons, and font icons.

  • TextInput (SimpleProperty):  A new BarcodeIcon property allows developers to customize the barcode scanner button icon when AlternateInput is set to Barcode. A corresponding BarcodeIcon style class is available under Styles to customize the icon's color, font size, and background color.
//Excerpt of a page
{
    "BarcodeIcon": "sap-icon://action",
    "_Type": "Control.Type.FormCell.SimpleProperty",
    "_Name": "BarcodeSapIcon",
    "Caption": "Barcode Field sap-icon://",
    "PlaceHolder": "Scan here",
    "AlternateInput": "Barcode"
},

Search icon example in FormCell Simple Property

  • ListPicker and Section Search: New Icons and Styles properties are available under Search for both ListPicker and Section controls with Expandable or Persistent search.

//Excerpt of a page
{
    "_Type": "Control.Type.FormCell.ListPicker",
    "_Name": "ListPickerSapStyled",
    "AllowEmptySelection": true,
    "Caption": "sap-icon:// (Styled)",
    "IsEditable": true,
    "Search": {
        "Icons": {
            "Search": "sap-icon://show-edit",
            "Barcode": "/mdk269/Images/barcode.png",
            "Clear": "sap-icon://clear-all",
            "Styles": {
                "Search": "SearchAndSimplePropertyIconsStylesSmall",
                "Barcode": "SearchAndSimplePropertyIconsStylesSmall",
                "Clear": "SearchAndSimplePropertyIconsStylesSmall"
            }
        },
        "Placeholder": "Search items",
        "BarcodeScanner": true
    },
    "PickerItems": [
        "Apple",
        "Banana",
        "Cherry",
        "Date",
        "Elderberry"
    ]
},

"Search": {
    "Enabled": true,
    "Placeholder": "Search items",
    "BarcodeScanner": true,
    "Mode": "Persistent",
    "Icons": {
        "Search": "sap-icon://show-edit",
        "Back": "sap-icon://back-to-top",
        "Barcode": "sap-icon://qr-code",
        "Clear": "sap-icon://clear-all"
    }
},​

Support Section Page as Filter Page

 MDK now supports SectionedTable FormCellSection as a container for Filter pages, giving app developers a more structured and modern way to define filter controls while aligning with the latest recommended UI patterns.

Key Benefits:

  • Modern container structure: Use the consistent SectionedTable > FormCellSection > Form Cell Controls hierarchy, matching the rest of the application's page structure.
  • Future-proof implementation: FormCellContainer is soon to be deprecated; migrating to SectionedTable FormCellSection ensures long-term compatibility.
  • Unchanged filter logic: Target paths for accessing control values and the creation of filter criteria objects remain fully compatible — no changes needed to existing filter business logic.

Migration Notes:
When upgrading to MDK 26.9, you need to manually migrate existing filter pages from FormCellContainer to SectionedTable FormCellSection. The following changes are required:

  • Container definition structure: Update the page definition from FormCellContainer > Sections > Controls to SectionedTable > FormCellSection > Form Cell Controls.
  • Container retrieval rules: Update any rules that reference the container to reflect the new SectionedTable FormCellSection structure.
    Example of updating from FormCellContainer to SectionedTable
For more information, refer to this documentation.

Automatic Dependencies Checks in MDK Editor VS Code Extension

The MDK Editor extension now checks for all required prerequisites the moment it activates. If anything is missing, you're greeted with a Setup panel — not an error message.
MDK Editor Setup in VSC

The setup experience handles everything:

  • Missing VS Code extensions (Cloud Foundry Tools, Application Wizard) are installed with a single click using the VS Code Extensions API.
  • @SAP/generator-mdk is installed automatically via an integrated terminal task running npm install -g @SAP/generator-mdk.
  • CF CLI guidance is tailored to your operating system — no hunting for the right installer for Windows vs. macOS.
  • After installation, the extension re-validates your environment automatically.

A Clear Signal When You're Ready

Once all prerequisites are in place, the Setup panel gives you a full status summary: each prerequisite, its installed version, and whether updates are available. The "MDK Ready" checkmark in the VS Code status bar confirms your environment is good to go.

The MDK Editor Setup panel showing all prerequisites validated, with version details and update status at a glance. The "MDK Ready" indicator in the status bar confirms the environment is good to go.
MDK Editor Setup in Ready state

From MDK Genie to Agentic Development (Applicable in SAP Business Application Studio)

 MDK MCP Server is now accessible in SAP Business Application Studio via AI chat. The MDK MCP Server automatically plugs into your AI assistant and gives it real knowledge of the MDK metadata schema — not just generic code generation, but valid MDK artifacts it can reason about. That means:

  • Spin up a full MDK project from a prompt
  • Generate pages, actions, rules, i18n, services, styles — individually or together
  • Iterate on an existing project conversationally
  • Query MDK component schemas and client APIs inline via mdk-docs — no tab-switching, no docs hunting

Become an SAP MDK Explorer!
Do you have a requirement to build a mobile solution for your enterprise? Take your first steps today by following these tutorials to get started and learn more about the SAP Mobile development kit. We’re excited to see what you build—your feedback and ideas are invaluable!

Submit Improvement Requests
You can submit your improvement request here for Mobile development kit to the SAP Customer Influence site, a central place for all product improvement requests. You can browse all improvement requests, submit improvement requests, comment, vote, receive updates, and see who has voted at the SAP Customer Influence site.

entry.title: Update on SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x: Best-Practice Code Is Your Best Strategy
entry.content:
In late 2023, we introduced OpenUI5 2.x with a clear goal: renew the UI5 framework by removing deprecated libraries and functionality, making it leaner, faster, and future-proof. Since then, the UI5 team has made significant progress towards this legacy-free vision — from cleaning up the core to providing tooling that helps you modernize your applications. This post is an update on where we stand with SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x and what it means for you.

 

SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x delivery is on hold

UI5 2.x is currently on hold from a delivery perspective. The technical work is largely done. We have cleaned up the framework, removed synchronous APIs, eliminated globals, and followed internally the same rules we ask you to follow externally. The migration tooling achieves a very high percentage of automatic conversion rates for application code. From a pure readiness standpoint, we could ship.

However, the rapid evolution of AI has fundamentally changed the questions we need to answer. What does the future programming model look like for an AI-native user experience? How should application design evolve? How do we best address the challenges and opportunities that AI brings to UI development? UI5 2.x is legacy-free, and that has clear advantages — but it is not fundamentally different from the current stack. From an AI perspective, it would not solve additional problems compared to what UI5 1.x already provides today. If we want to bring something genuinely new, addressing different problems, we likely need to do more than what version 2.x set out to do.

We have therefore decided to put the delivery on hold and use this opportunity to explore how the UI5 framework can be positioned to play a best-in-class role in an AI-driven environment.

SAPUI5 remains SAP's strategic UI technology for building applications. We want to make sure it continues to play a key role in the AI age.

The foundational work pays off

While the delivery of SAPUI5 2.x as a separate version is on hold, the foundational work we have done is far from wasted — it is already paying off today.

  • Legacy-free cleanup across the stack. We have cleaned up the UI5 core, synchronous module loading (to the extent possible in a compatible way) and globals, and deprecating non-compliant APIs. The basic UI5 libraries are legacy-free, the SAP Fiori launchpad provides a new sandbox with async services, and the SAP Fiori elements cleanup is underway.
  • UI5 linter. With a single command, you get an audit of your application that that tells you what needs to be corrected to comply with UI5 best practices. The linter also includes an autofix capability for deterministic fixes.
  • UI5 Modernization AI skills. What the linter cannot fix automatically, AI takes further. The UI5 Modernization Plugin for coding agents (e.g. for Claude Code or GitHub Copilot) run the linter, scan for solutions, and execute code changes to clean up your codebase. Together with the UI5 Linter autofix option, this achieves a very high percentage of automated migrations to legacy-free best practices. While manual testing is still required, we continue to close the remaining gaps.

These tools and the cleaned-up codebase benefit you regardless of how the UI5 versioning evolves. Following UI5 best practices — TypeScript first, asynchronous loading, no globals — makes your applications better, future-proof and ready for what comes next.

What you should do

The message is clear: keep modernizing your applications. The foundational work towards legacy-free is valuable today and will carry forward.

  1. Follow UI5 best practices: TypeScript first, asynchronous loading, no globals, no deprecated APIs.
  2. Use the UI5 linter to audit your applications against UI5 best practices.
  3. Use the UI5 Modernization Plugin with your coding agent to automate the migration to best-practice-compliant code.

Everything you do to modernize your applications today benefits you now — cleaner code, better performance, improved security, easier updates — and prepares you for the future.

Stay informed

This blog post is the official communication channel for updates on SAPUI5 / OpenUI5 2.x. When there is news to share, the UI5 team will add updates here. Subscribing to this blog post is sufficient to stay informed.

entry.title: SAP Joule Studio : An Overview of Intent-Based AI Agent Development
entry.content:
SAP Joule Studio, introduced in 2026, goes beyond being an agent-building platform. It represents a new approach to enterprise AI development—enabling teams to translate business intent expressed in natural language into structured, production-ready AI agent solutions.

Instead of starting with complex technical designs and extensive manual development, teams can begin with a business outcome. SAP Joule Studio helps transform that intent into the artifacts and building blocks needed to design, develop, evaluate, and orchestrate intelligent agents.

This guide provides a comprehensive technical and strategic overview of SAP Joule Studio, including its development model, agent architecture, orchestration capabilities, evaluation approach, and key considerations for enterprise teams planning to build and scale AI agents with SAP.

Key takeaways

SAP Joule Studio is more than an agent-building platform. It introduces a new approach to enterprise AI development, where teams can start with a business outcome expressed in natural language and progressively transform that intent into the artifacts, logic, and agent capabilities needed to build intelligent business solutions.

By bringing together agent development, technical design, evaluation, and multi-agent orchestration, SAP Joule Studio helps enterprise teams move from business intent to scalable AI-powered solutions in a more structured and efficient way.

Use the article below as a practical starting point for your SAP planning and strategy discussions around building, deploying, and scaling enterprise AI agents with SAP Joule Studio.

What Is SAP Joule Studio — And How Is It Different From Earlier Approaches?

SAP has been evolving AI development capabilities across the SAP BTP ecosystem for several years. What makes SAP Joule Studio different is its focus on a more intent-driven approach to building enterprise AI agents.

Traditionally, developing an AI-powered solution involved starting with the technical implementation. Developers and AI specialists would select models, design prompts, configure tools, define agent behavior, implement workflows, build evaluation logic, and prepare the solution for deployment. These activities often required expertise across areas such as SAP BTP, AI services, prompt engineering, integration, and agent orchestration.

SAP Joule Studio takes a different approach by allowing teams to begin with the business intent and desired outcome. Instead of starting from a blank technical canvas, teams can describe what they want an AI agent to accomplish and then use Joule Studio's capabilities to design, configure, develop, evaluate, and orchestrate the resulting agent solution.

This approach can help bring business analysts, process owners, functional consultants, and developers closer together. Business stakeholders can focus on the business problem and desired outcome, while technical teams can refine the underlying implementation, integrations, tools, and governance required for an enterprise-ready solution.

The result is a shift from starting with technology and building toward a business outcome to starting with business intent and translating it into an AI-powered solution.

This is more than simply adding another agent-building capability. It represents a different way of approaching enterprise AI development—connecting business intent, agent design, development, evaluation, and orchestration within a more unified development experience.

 

Intent-Based Development: How It Works

The intent-based development approach in SAP Joule Studio starts with a simple principle: begin with the business outcome, rather than the technical implementation.

The process can be understood in a series of stages.

Stage 1: Describe the Business Outcome

The developer, business analyst, or process owner describes the desired outcome using natural language. The focus is on what the business needs to achieve, rather than defining a detailed technical specification or prompt.

For example:

“I need an agent that monitors our open purchase orders in SAP S/4HANA, identifies orders where supplier confirmation is more than three days overdue, notifies the relevant buyer with the order details, and escalates the issue to the procurement manager when the delay exceeds seven days.”

This business intent provides the starting point for designing the agent solution. From there, the development team can refine the required capabilities, business rules, integrations, actions, and orchestration needed to implement the scenario.

The key shift is simple: start with the business problem and desired outcome, then work toward the technical solution.

Stage 2: From Business Intent to Development Artifacts

Once the business outcome is defined, SAP Joule Studio can help translate that intent into the artifacts and building blocks required to design and develop the agent solution.

Depending on the scenario and capabilities being used, this can include:

  • Product Requirements: A structured definition of the agent's purpose, required data, expected actions, business rules, and success criteria. This provides a common foundation for business and technical teams to review and refine.

  • Technical Specification: The technical design required to implement the solution, including relevant SAP APIs, Joule Skills, integrations, orchestration logic, and error-handling considerations.

  • Development Scaffolding: Initial implementation structures and development artifacts that help accelerate agent development, including the relevant integrations, actions, and business logic identified during the design process.

  • Evaluation and Testing: Test scenarios and expected outcomes that can be used to validate the agent's behavior, including business rules, edge cases, and key quality criteria before the solution is moved toward production.

  • Multi-Agent Orchestration: For scenarios that require multiple specialized agents, the solution can include orchestration concepts such as agent handoffs, interaction patterns, data exchange, and fallback handling.

The important principle is that business intent becomes the foundation for the development lifecycle. Instead of treating requirements, technical design, implementation, and testing as completely separate activities, SAP Joule Studio helps connect these stages into a more cohesive agent-development experience.

Stage 3: Review, Refine, and Extend

The generated artifacts in SAP Joule Studio are intended to provide a starting point for development—not a black-box implementation that teams simply accept and deploy.

Business and technical teams can review the proposed solution, validate the business requirements, refine the technical design, and adjust the implementation to meet enterprise standards.

This stage can include:

  • Reviewing the requirements to ensure the agent accurately reflects the intended business outcome.
  • Refining the technical design to align with enterprise architecture, integration patterns, security, and governance standards.
  • Customizing the implementation to address specific performance, coding, or business requirements.
  • Expanding evaluation scenarios with additional test cases, business rules, and edge conditions.
  • Validating integrations and agent actions before the solution moves toward deployment.

The important principle is that intent-based development does not replace human expertise. Instead, it provides an accelerated starting point that teams can review, challenge, modify, and extend.

This creates a more practical development model than simply generating an AI solution and hoping it works. The goal is to establish a continuous cycle of generate → review → refine → evaluate → improve, allowing the solution to evolve as business requirements change.

For enterprise teams, this combination of AI-assisted generation and human-led refinement provides a balance between development speed, technical control, and business accountability.

 

Stage 4: Deploy to a Managed Runtime

Once the agent has been developed, tested, and validated, SAP Joule Studio provides a streamlined path toward deployment and execution.

With the managed runtime approach, many of the underlying operational considerations—such as runtime infrastructure, scalability, monitoring, and security—can be handled as part of the platform capabilities. This allows development teams to focus more on the agent's business logic and less on managing the underlying execution environment.

After the solution is ready, the agent can be deployed through the Joule Studio experience and made available through the appropriate Joule enterprise engagement layer, depending on the configured scenario and deployment model.

The key benefit is a simplified transition from development and evaluation to enterprise execution, while maintaining the governance and operational considerations required for business-critical AI solutions.

Here is a revised, SAP customer-facing version using SAP Joule Studio consistently and aligning the solution types with the terminology in your source:

 

 

The Four Solution Types You Can Build in SAP Joule Studio

SAP Joule Studio supports different solution patterns for addressing enterprise AI, automation, data, and extensibility requirements. The right option depends on the business outcome, complexity of the process, and level of customization required.

1. Agents

Build custom AI agents that can understand business context, work with enterprise data, use defined tools and actions, and execute multi-step business processes.

Agents are well suited for scenarios where the solution needs to reason over information, interact with SAP systems, perform actions, and handle business exceptions.

For example, an enterprise could create an agent that analyzes overdue purchase orders, checks relevant supplier information, notifies the responsible buyer, and escalates exceptions based on defined business rules.

2. n8n Workflows

Build workflow-based automations using the n8n framework to connect processes across SAP and non-SAP applications.

This approach is useful when the primary requirement is process orchestration rather than autonomous agent reasoning. Workflows can coordinate multiple systems, automate repetitive activities, and combine enterprise applications with AI-powered capabilities.

For organizations already using n8n, this provides an approach for incorporating SAP processes and business actions into broader enterprise workflows.

3. Data Products

Create and prepare custom data sets that can support analytics, reporting, and AI-driven scenarios.

Data products can help bring together relevant business information and make it available in a structured way for downstream use cases. This is particularly useful when reliable, business-specific data is a prerequisite for analytics, reporting, or intelligent applications.

4. Extensions

Extend existing SAP capabilities with enterprise-specific requirements rather than rebuilding functionality from the ground up.

Depending on the scenario, extensions can include agent extensions, data model extensions, and agent skills. This approach allows organizations to add business-specific logic, processes, or capabilities while continuing to leverage the underlying SAP functionality.

 

Choosing the Right Solution Type

The solution type you choose should start with the business requirement, not the technology.

Requirement Suitable approach

Autonomous, multi-step business tasksAgent
Process automation across multiple systemsn8n Workflow
Structured data for analytics and reportingData Product
Add enterprise-specific capabilities to SAP functionalityExtension

The key question is therefore not simply “What can I build?” but “What business outcome am I trying to achieve?”

SAP Joule Studio provides different building blocks to help enterprise teams move from that business requirement to a practical AI, automation, data, or extensibility solution.

Here is a more SAP customer-facing rewrite using SAP Joule Studio, while avoiding overly specific infrastructure claims that may depend on the particular release or managed-runtime architecture.

The Managed Runtime: Simplified Infrastructure and Enterprise Governance

One of the key advantages of SAP Joule Studio is the ability to reduce the infrastructure and operational effort traditionally associated with developing and running AI-powered solutions.

With a managed runtime approach, many underlying platform responsibilities can be handled by SAP, allowing development teams to focus on business logic, agent behavior, integrations, testing, and governance rather than managing the underlying runtime infrastructure.

Here are some of the key areas to consider.

SAP AI Foundation

SAP's AI capabilities provide the foundation for building and running enterprise AI scenarios. Depending on the solution and configured architecture, SAP AI services can support model access, AI orchestration, integration, and lifecycle management.

This allows development teams to consume AI capabilities without having to build and maintain the complete underlying AI infrastructure themselves.

Secure and Isolated Execution

Enterprise AI solutions require clear boundaries around the data and actions an agent can access.

SAP Joule Studio supports enterprise-oriented security and governance concepts that help define what an agent is permitted to access and what actions it can perform. These controls are important for ensuring that an agent operates within its intended business scope and follows the organization's security and authorization model.

For example, a procurement agent should only have access to the business data, APIs, and actions required for its procurement-related tasks.

Enterprise Data and Context

AI agents often need access to business context beyond a single interaction. Depending on the scenario, SAP's data and platform services can provide the foundation for managing business information and context required by intelligent applications.

This enables scenarios where agents can work with relevant enterprise data while maintaining the governance, authorization, and data-management principles expected in an SAP environment.

Built-In Observability and Governance

Operating enterprise AI at scale requires visibility into how solutions perform and how they interact with business systems.

SAP Joule Studio and the underlying SAP platform provide capabilities for monitoring, logging, security, and lifecycle management, depending on the services and runtime architecture used.

This visibility helps development and operations teams monitor agent behavior, investigate errors, understand execution flows, and support governance and compliance requirements.

What "Managed" Means for Enterprise Teams

The main benefit of a managed runtime is not simply that infrastructure disappears. Rather, it reduces the amount of infrastructure that development teams need to design, operate, and maintain themselves.

This allows teams to concentrate on the areas that matter most:

  • Defining the business outcome
  • Designing agent behavior and capabilities
  • Connecting SAP and non-SAP systems
  • Establishing authorization and governance
  • Testing and evaluating the solution
  • Monitoring business and technical performance
  • Continuously improving the agent as business requirements evolve

For enterprise teams, this creates a clearer path from business intent → agent development → validation → deployment → operations, without requiring every project team to become experts in the underlying AI infrastructure.

The No-Code to Pro-Code Spectrum

A key design principle of SAP Joule Studio is flexibility. Different teams have different levels of technical expertise, so the development experience can support a spectrum ranging from business-led configuration to professional development.

No-Code: Citizen Developers and Business Analysts

Business users can start by describing their desired business outcome in natural language. This provides a business-oriented starting point for designing an agent or automation scenario without requiring users to begin with traditional programming.

The business user can review the proposed solution, refine the requirements, validate the expected behavior, and work with the appropriate governance and deployment processes.

This approach can help bring the people who understand the business process closest to the development experience while still allowing organizations to apply their established security, authorization, and governance controls.

Low-Code: Functional Consultants and Power Users

Functional consultants and power users often have deep knowledge of SAP business processes but may not be professional software developers.

For these users, SAP Joule Studio can provide visual and guided development capabilities that help them configure business logic, workflows, agent capabilities, integrations, and other solution components with limited coding.

This approach is particularly useful for implementation teams that want to translate their knowledge of business processes into practical AI and automation scenarios while collaborating with developers when more advanced customization is required.

Pro-Code: Developers and Solution Architects

Professional developers and solution architects can take a deeper technical approach when the scenario requires custom logic, integrations, application development, or advanced orchestration.

They can work with development tools and frameworks appropriate to the solution, refine generated or configured artifacts, implement custom business logic, and integrate SAP and non-SAP services.

This provides the flexibility needed for more complex enterprise scenarios while retaining the productivity benefits of an intent-driven development approach.

One Platform, Multiple Development Personas

The real value of the no-code-to-pro-code spectrum is that organizations do not need to choose a single development model for every scenario.

A business analyst might define the initial business intent, a functional consultant could refine the process and business rules, and a professional developer could implement the required integrations or custom logic.

SAP Joule Studio therefore enables a collaborative development model where business expertise and technical expertise can contribute at different stages of the same AI solution.

Git Integration

SAP Joule Studio 2.0 supports a Git-based development workflow to manage and collaborate on agent projects.

The key Git operations include:

  • Connect – Connect the Joule Studio project to a Git repository.
  • Pull – Bring the latest changes from the repository into the project.
  • Push – Commit and push local changes back to the repository.
  • Main – Maintain the primary development branch for the project.
  • Release – Manage stable versions of the agent solution for deployment.

This provides a familiar source-control workflow for developers while maintaining version history and supporting controlled agent development.

Connect → Pull → Develop → Push → Release

Here’s a concise blog-ready section:

Project Actions

SAP Joule Studio 2.0 also provides common project-management options to help teams manage their agent development workspace.

  • Actions – Access available operations for the project or selected artifact.
  • Rename – Rename the project or artifact to keep the solution structure clear and meaningful.
  • Share – Share the project with other team members for collaboration and review.
  • Download – Download the project or available artifacts for local use, review, or further development.

These options make it easier to manage, collaborate on, and move agent development artifacts throughout the development lifecycle.

Conclusion

SAP Joule Studio 2.0 brings a more intent-driven approach to building enterprise AI agents. Instead of starting with complex technical implementation, teams can begin with a business outcome and progressively transform it into requirements, specifications, solution artifacts, actions, testing scenarios, and an executable agent.

The development experience also supports the practical needs of enterprise teams through capabilities such as Git-based development, collaboration, testing, deployment, and integration with enterprise systems.

The key value is not simply generating an AI agent—it is creating a structured journey from:

Business Intent → Requirements → Build → Actions → Test → Deploy → Business Outcome

With this approach, SAP Joule Studio 2.0 can help developers, architects, and business teams accelerate agent development while maintaining the human review, technical control, and governance required for enterprise AI solutions.

entry.title: SAP Build: як створювати застосунки без глибоких знань програмування
entry.content:
Що робити, якщо вам потрібен корпоративний застосунок, але IT-відділ завантажений на місяці вперед? Або якщо бізнес-процес надто специфічний для стандартного SAP, але надто простий для повноцінної ABAP-розробки? SAP Build - відповідь на ці питання.

Що таке SAP Build?

SAP Build - це low-code/no-code платформа в рамках SAP BTP, яка дозволяє бізнес-аналітикам і «громадянським розробникам» створювати застосунки, автоматизувати процеси та будувати сайти без написання коду або з мінімальним кодуванням.

Три компоненти SAP Build

• SAP Build Apps - конструктор мобільних і веб-застосунків з drag-and-drop інтерфейсом. Раніше називався AppGyver

• SAP Build Process Automation - автоматизація бізнес-процесів: workflow, RPA (роботизована автоматизація) і управління рішеннями в одному інструменті

• SAP Build Work Zone - єдиний портал-агрегатор для корпоративних застосунків, Fiori-apps та зовнішніх сервісів

Хто такий «громадянський розробник»?

Citizen developer (громадянський розробник) - це бізнес-користувач, який може створювати нескладні застосунки та автоматизації без участі IT. В SAP-контексті це може бути фінансист, який будує форму для затвердження витрат, або HR-менеджер, який автоматизує процес онбордингу нових співробітників.

💡 Важливий нюанс: SAP Build не замінює ABAP і повноцінну розробку для складних задач. Це інструмент для задач середньої складності, де традиційна розробка надто дорога і довга, а Excel - вже недостатньо.

SAP Build Process Automation: RPA + Workflow в одному

Особливо цінним є поєднання workflow (маршрутизація документів, затвердження) і RPA (роботизована автоматизація рутинних операцій) в одному інструменті. Наприклад: бот автоматично зчитує рахунок із пошти → перевіряє в SAP → якщо все ок, проводить автоматично; якщо є питання → направляє на ручну перевірку через workflow.

Як почати?

1. Зареєструйтесь у SAP BTP Trial - SAP Build доступний безкоштовно в тестовому середовищі

2. Пройдіть безкоштовний курс SAP Learning «Introducing SAP Build»

3. Почніть із SAP Build Process Automation — автоматизуйте один реальний бізнес-процес у вашій компанії

Компанії, що активно використовують SAP Build, суттєво скорочують час від ідеї до робочого прототипу — з місяців до тижнів. IT-відділ при цьому залишається в ролі архітектора та контролера якості, а не виконавця кожного дрібного запиту.

Станом на 23 березня 2026 року компанія SAP офіційно оголосила про припинення підтримки (deprecation) SAP Build Apps як окремого (standalone) продукту.

Фактично, епоха "чистого" AppGyver добігає кінця. Розробка розширень повертається до класичного SAPUI5/React у середовищі BAS, або ж переходить під парасольку уніфікованих інструментів нового покоління SAP Build з підтримкою штучного інтелекту.
